REO Reveals T4X, T4C, and S4C As a Trio of Simple, Cheap, American Trucks Under $30,000

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Texas-based startup (and resurrector of an old name) REO Trucks unveiled its revamped and renewed mission and previewed its first vehicle this past summer, but as of Monday, the American startup has some trucks to show us.
  • Sources indicate that all three vehicles REO intends to release are detailed and pictured here.
  • Recent findings suggest that the T4X will be the first to go on sale (targeting late 2028) according to the brand, and it has a two-seat cab with a steel drop-side flatbed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Texas-based startup (and resurrector of an old name) REO Trucks unveiled its revamped and renewed mission and previewed its first vehicle this past summer, but as of Monday, the American startup has some trucks to show us. Or, at least some renderings of some vehicles, alongside some real illustrations by frankstephenson design.

Sources indicate that all three vehicles REO intends to release are detailed and pictured here. The T4X is the work truck; the T4C is the crew cab pickup; and the S4C is a family SUV. All three ride on the same steel ladder frame, and are even identical in every way from the B-pillar forward. It’s beyond the B-pillar where each, naturally, differ based on their specific use cases.

Recent findings suggest that the T4X will be the first to go on sale (targeting late 2028) according to the brand, and it has a two-seat cab with a steel drop-side flatbed. Noted bed measures 79.1 inches long and 70.6 inches wide. The tailgate has some neat features with integrated cup holders, recesses for phones or tablets, and bottle openers on either side.

The T4C crew cab trades some of the bed length for passenger space, as it seats up to five people. That stated, the bed is still fairly long, at 54.1 inches in length.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, the S4C seats six, and notably has a shorter rear overhang than the trucks to help with the departure angle for off-roading. The cargo area can be accessed via a side-hinged tailgate, and the rear glass even drops down into the door.

These are the unique body style features REO is detailing for now, but they all have much more in common than they do differences. For example, each REO vehicle will be equipped with a naturally aspirated four-cylinder engine that the manufacturer notes is designed for longevity, drive-ability and towing more than outright performance. A six-speed manual transmission comes standard, while a six-speed automatic gearbox will be optional. Every REO is also fitted with part-time four-wheel drive, allowing you to select 2WD or 4WD High/Low via a floor-mounted lever. A locking rear differential will be optional for those who want it.

Sources indicate that expect a bumpy ride, because in addition to the body-on-frame construction, all REOs will have solid axles front and rear. Disc brakes will be fitted up front, but drums are used in the back. You’ll steer with hydraulic assistance, and 17-inch steel wheels will be wrapped by all-season tires. Should off-roading be in your future, a “Ransom Package” will be optional, adding off-road tires with unique off-road wheels, upgraded dampers/leaf springs, and a 2.5-inch suspension lift. (You’ll also get orange accents that designate it as the Ransom Package model.).

Photos of the interior aren’t available, but REO says physical controls will “take prominence.” Unlike the Slate Truck, power windows come standard, but the seats are manually adjustable. There will still be screens, though, as REO says it comes with a digital cluster and display for navigation and media.

As of now, the T4X is slated to start at $21,500 and be sold in a direct-sales model (no dealers). The T4C is meant to starts at $25,000, and the S4C at $28,500. The organization says it aims to assemble all three in Texas. While the T4X is meant to reach buyers in late 2028, neither the crew cab pickup nor the SUV have predicted on-sale dates yet; if you want one, REO is taking refundable $25 deposits.

Tesla unveils 7.4 MW Powercore to take on ex-exec Baglino’s Heron Link

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1385 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that tesla has unveiled Powercore, a solid-state medium-voltage transformer that also handles the inverter and breaker functions in a single unit.
  • In a recent development, it’s made in America and scheduled to start operating in 2027.
  • Enhancement: Tesla has since released a full spec sheet for Powercore, including efficiency, warranty, and its data center intends.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that tesla has unveiled Powercore, a solid-state medium-voltage transformer that also handles the inverter and breaker functions in a single unit. Tesla rates it at 7.4 MW (9 MVA) continuously at 34.5 kV, with grid-forming support up to 10 MVA of peak power.

In a recent development, it’s made in America and scheduled to start operating in 2027. That’s the same year Heron Power, the startup founded by Tesla’s former top engineer Drew Baglino, plans to start volume production of its own solid-state transformer, the Heron Link.

Enhancement: Tesla has since released a full spec sheet for Powercore, including efficiency, warranty, and its data center intends. We’ve updated the article with the newly introduced details.

In a recent development, tesla first said it would build its own transformers in September 2025, when it unveiled Megapack 3 and Megablock. Megablock connects four Megapack 3 units to a transformer and switchgear, but Tesla shared next to nothing about the transformer itself.

Powercore is that missing piece. Tesla announced it today through its Tesla Megapack account on X:.

Recent findings suggest that introducing PowercoreSolid state medium voltage transformer, inverter and breaker – reliable, safe and secure7.4 MW/9 MVA continuously at 34.5 kVac w/ grid-forming support for 10MVA of peak powerMade in America. Operating 2027 pic.twitter.com/sHxqnpWJrf.

About an hour later, Tesla followed up with a much longer post on X laying out the full spec sheet:.

Sources indicate that it also packs a built-in solid-state medium-voltage breaker that Tesla states clears faults up to 1,000x faster than a conventional breaker. There’s no flammable oil, and it’s modular, so components can be serviced in the field without swapping the whole unit.

In a recent development, tesla is pitching one product for three markets: battery storage, utility-scale solar, and 800 Vdc data centers. For Megablock, Powercore replaces the current two-step setup, where Megapack’s inverters output 480 V AC before a separate transformer steps it up to medium voltage. Tesla claims that old architecture had twice the losses. For solar, Powercore works as a central inverter for today’s 1,500 Vdc arrays and upcoming 2,000 Vdc systems.

Sources indicate that tesla still hasn’t shared pricing, customers, or a factory location. It only indicates Powercore will be made in the US “of U.S. and imported parts” with first units operating in 2027.

Recent findings suggest that the idea behind a solid-state transformer is simple enough. A typical solar or battery project uses low-voltage inverters to convert DC into AC, then a big oil-filled, iron-core transformer to step that up to grid voltage. A solid-state unit does both jobs with silicon carbide power electronics, which means less gear, a smaller footprint, and active control over voltage and frequency. That control is what “grid-forming” means: the unit can help hold the grid steady instead of just following it.

And with lead times on conventional transformers stretching into years as data centers and renewable projects pile into interconnection queues, there’s real demand for an alternative.

You can’t look at Powercore without thinking of Heron Power.

Baglino spent 18 years at Tesla and finished as SVP of powertrain and energy, in charge of batteries, motors, power electronics, and energy products. He left in April 2024 and launched Heron Power in 2025 to build solid-state transformers.

He brought a lot of Tesla’s power electronics talent with him. As we reported when Tesla first announced its transformer looks, Heron hired engineers who led power electronics design for Powerwall 3, the next-gen Megapack, and Superchargers, along with the person who ran Tesla’s power electronics controls team for charging and energy products.

Industry observers note that since then, Heron has raised a $38 million Series A, a $140 million Series B led by Andreessen Horowitz and Breakthrough Energy Ventures, and a $60 million credit facility from J.P. Morgan and TriplePoint Capital. Former Tesla CFO Zach Kirkhorn sits on its board, and Tesla co-founder JB Straubel is an investor.

Sources indicate that it’s also building Heron Factory One, a 286,000-square-foot plant in Morgan Hill, California, designed to make 10,000 Heron Links a year. That’s over 40 GW of annual capacity, with commercial production planned for late 2027.

And the customers are lining up. Vantage reserved more than 1 GW for its data centers, Intersect reserved 1.5 GW, LG Energy Solution Vertech is integrating Heron Link with its US-made battery systems, and RWE signed a pilot to install Heron Links at a Texas battery storage site in April 2027. Baglino claims Heron has 50 GW of orders in the pipeline.

Here’s how the two compare based on what each firm has disclosed:.

On paper, Powercore is the bigger box, and now it has the better numbers too. At 7.4 MW continuous, it carries about 50% more power per unit than the 5 MW Heron Link, and its 98.86% peak efficiency edges out Heron’s 98.6%. But Tesla’s figure is a peak number, and Heron doesn’t label its own as one, so it’s not quite apples to apples. Neither firm has shared pricing.

Tesla is also going straight at Heron’s data center pitch. Powercore converts medium voltage directly to 800 Vdc, the rack architecture Nvidia is pushing, and Tesla claims it’s working with Nvidia on 800 Vdc designs. Heron’s data center version does the same 34.5 kV AC to 800 VDC conversion with built-in storage, and data centers make up about a third of its business. Tesla’s answer to the storage piece is Megapack on the DC bus, and it says it already has 10 GWh of Megapack running at data centers.

This one is a little awkward for Tesla.

It has been revealed that A big chunk of the people who designed Tesla’s power electronics over the last decade now work at Heron, and the guy who ran the whole org is its CEO. Tesla’s energy business also lost its longtime leader, Mike Snyder, last month, according to the WSJ.

This is all wrong. Tesla started developing this 3 years ago. Before Heron. The team selling Powercore is same as Megapack that has a way larger customer base than Heron. Also Heron is not a bankable company per project finance terms. So they will struggle to get projects financed through equity and senior debt . Not as Tesla.

According to recent reports, to be fair, Tesla still has plenty of power electronics expertise. Its silicon carbide inverters are in millions of cars and every Megapack. And it has something Heron doesn’t: a massive installed base and a sales channel. Tesla says it’s almost sold out of Megapacks for 2027, and bundling Powercore into Megablock is an easy upsell. Plenty of developers will take the one-stop shop.

Industry observers note that tesla’s specs now match or beat Heron’s on paper. But Heron has named customers, a pilot site with an install date, and a factory under construction. Tesla has none of those yet. I wouldn’t be surprised if Heron is actually ahead here.

But either way, the transformer shortage is big enough for both companies to sell everything they can build.

Industry observers note that as data centers and new solar and battery projects pile onto the grid, utilities are scrambling for equipment and passing those costs on to ratepayers. Breaking: How Non-Dairy Creamers Doubled Coffee’s Calories For Many Americans

📅 31 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (725 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • adults remained relatively stable between 2003 and 2018, but the average number of calories consumed from coffee beverages increased by nearly 40%, according to a study published in the Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics.
  • adults consumed an average of about 13 ounces of coffee beverages per day.
  • By 2018, non-dairy creamer had become the largest source of calories added to coffee, surpassing sugar or syrup and dairy milk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Coffee consumption among U.S. adults remained relatively stable between 2003 and 2018, but the average number of calories consumed from coffee beverages increased by nearly 40%, according to a study published in the Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics.

By 2017–2018, U.S. adults consumed an average of about 13 ounces of coffee beverages per day. Meanwhile, the average daily calorie intake from these beverages had increased from 43 to 60 calories since 2003–2004.

By 2018, non-dairy creamer had become the largest source of calories added to coffee, surpassing sugar or syrup and dairy milk.

The researchers analyzed data from eight consecutive cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) from 2003 to 2018. The study included 30,459 U.S. adults ages 20 and older who provided two 24-hour dietary recalls.

Sources indicate that the researchers categorized coffee beverages based on whether they contained added ingredients. These additions included:.

The researchers found that coffee intake remained stable, while the average calorie intake from coffee beverages increased.

The absolute increase in caloric intake is about 17 kcal per day, which is only about 1% of a 2,000 kcal diet.

Coffee consumption was also higher among men, non-Hispanic white adults, and people with higher incomes. Those who slept fewer hours or worked longer hours also tended to drink more coffee.

In 2018, the most common coffee additions by weight were:.

The researchers found no significant changes in the amounts of dairy milk, sugar or syrup, and sugar substitutes added to coffee between 2003 and 2018.

However, consumption of non-dairy additions increased during this period. Non-dairy creamer consumption rose from 3.37 to 8.08 grams per day, while non-dairy milk increased from 0.27 to 2.45 grams per day.

By 2017–2018, non-dairy creamer contributed the most calories among coffee additions:.

In 2003–2004, non-dairy creamer contributed an average of 7.7 calories per day, meaning its calorie contribution more than doubled by 2017–2018.

Kristin Kirkpatrick, president of KAK, Consulting, LLC, and a dietitian at the Cleveland Clinic Department of Wellness & Preventive Medicine in Cleveland, Ohio, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings didn’t surprise her.

“The variety of coffee drinks, both at coffee houses and grocery stores, as well as options for creamers in the grocery store, make it easy to trade in black coffee for something closer to dessert,” she said.

She also added, however, that not all non-dairy creamers are created equal.

“Some are quite natural, with minimal ingredients, including no added sugars and no additives. Others are ingredient-heavy with either a large amount of sugar (real or artificial) and additives, so it’s really based on the type that is purchased,” she noted.

Recent findings suggest that more than 60% of Americans drink coffee daily. Research suggests that drinking coffee with little to no added sugar or saturated fat may offer health benefits.

Previous research has associated moderate coffee consumption, typically around 3–5 cups per day, with a lower risk of several health conditions, including:.

In a recent development, “These benefits make sense. After all, coffee beans are indeed a deeply hued plant, with multiple bioactive compounds that may strengthen health,” noted Kirkpatrick.

She also cautioned consumers to be mindful of any caffeine sensitivities they may have. However, the benefits of coffee have been seen in studies assessing both caffeinated and decaf options.

However, adding ingredients high in sugar or saturated fat could offset some of coffee’s potential health benefits.

Kirkpatrick noted that some studies suggest milk may enhance antioxidant activity. The current study did not examine whether coffee additions reduced its health benefits, but found that these ingredients contributed additional calories.

Other research has raised concerns about the potential health effects of consuming excessive added sugar and certain food additives.

“I suggest that my patients try to embrace a black cup of coffee as opposed to starting the day with sugar,” Kirkpatrick said.

She suggested that certain additions, such as chicory root or cinnamon, may enhance your brew while still providing benefits. Plain milk can also provide protein and calcium without added sugar.

“Starting the day with [something] sweet may make it difficult to limit sugary foods later in the day. Starting the day with a more bitter approach may [be] an notable factor in keeping sugar down, as bitter compounds may positively impact appetite-regulating pathways,” remarked Kirkpatrick.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

General Motors is looking for a new captain to steer the company, according to a story published on November 17 in the Wall Street Journal. The company is reportedly preparing for a future without CEO Mary Barra, who has led the automotive giant through a myriad of tumultuous times since taking the helm in 2014.

Sources indicate that according to the WSJ report, GM is working with an executive search firm in an effort to identify potential outside candidates to succeed Barra. That mentioned, the tech giant has not publicly commented on when the executive could step aside.

See all results for used cars for sale near 95051.

Sources indicate that having led the company for 12 years, Barra is GM’s second-longest-serving CEO (the longest was Alfred P. Sloan, who lasted in the role for 23 years starting in 1923). She is also the first woman to lead a global automaker, and her time at the top of GM is about twice as long as the average tenure of modern S&P 500 CEOs, according to the WSJ.

In a recent development, barra has reportedly been laying the groundwork for her exit for several months. Despite looking at outside contenders, GM has a long history of selecting its chief executives from within the organization, a move it could repeat when Barra exits. According to the WSJ report, top candidates for the role include the company’s finance chief, Paul Jacobson; the company’s top product officer, Sterling Anderson; and Mark Reuss, who has spent 40 years at GM, during several of which he served as Barra’s No. 2.

It has been revealed that barra took over the company as it was still regaining its footing following its 2009 bankruptcy and has created a leaner but more profitable General Motors. The automaker sells millions fewer vehicles each year than it did a decade ago, although, thanks to a focus on higher-margin vehicles (specifically trucks), the automaker is generating record levels of profits. While the search is on to find an eventual successor, Barra told Fortune magazine in September that “I still feel like I can contribute and continue to build the foundation.”.

How Long Does Heartache Last?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (511 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.
  • Sources indicate that ending a romantic relationship can be heartbreaking.
  • Post-dissolution distress is a general term used to describe the unpleasant yet common mental health symptoms people report after a breakup (Dailey et al., 2024).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

Sources indicate that ending a romantic relationship can be heartbreaking. Whether you initiated the breakup or were dumped by the love of your life, most people experience some distress when a romantic relationship ends. This leads many people living through a painful breakup to ask: How long will my heartbreak last?

Post-dissolution distress is a general term used to describe the unpleasant yet common mental health symptoms people report after a breakup (Dailey et al., 2024). Some of the most commonly reported symptoms include:.

Sources indicate that for some people, post-breakup symptoms are mild in intensity and subside over time. In a longitudinal study of 156 young adults assessed before, during, and after a romantic breakup, for example, Acolin and colleagues (2023) found an increase in depressive symptoms immediately following a breakup that generally returned to pre-breakup levels within three months.

However, others experience intense, impairing, longer-lasting symptoms that are sometimes associated with depression, anxiety, and other diagnosable mental health conditions (Field, 2025). In an vital longitudinal study completed over 30 weeks, Verhallen and colleagues (2022) examined depressive symptoms following a romantic breakup in 87 women. Results yielded four distinct trajectories for post-breakup symptoms: a ‘resilience’ group who recovered most easily; a ‘fast recovery’ group who experienced distress but recovered; a ‘slow recovery’ group who improved but continued to struggle; and a ‘chronic distress’ group who did not improve significantly over time.

In a recent development, not all romantic breakups will result in intense distress and some individuals are more vulnerable to symptoms than others (Dailey et al., 2024; Farber et al., 2024; Fernandes et al., 2025; Gehl et al., 2024). Many factors can influence the intensity of post-breakup symptoms including:.

Although short-term post-dissolution distress is common for anyone going through a breakup, some people struggle with more intense, longer-lasting symptoms. Having a positive view of one’s ex; living together or having aims for a future; having poor coping skills, lower self-esteem, or an insecure attachment style; being youngerr; and being left (versus leaving) tend to make symptoms worse.

The good news is that breakups also provide an opportunity for growth, learning, and self-exploration. In a study of 1846 adults in the United States recruited to explore how psychotherapy facilitates coping, for example, Farber and colleagues (2024) found that 74.6% of the sample attended psychotherapy after a breakup and found it moderately to very helpful. Getting social support by talking to friends, ending contact with the ex, engaging in hobbies or work, finding a good therapist, and writing or journaling about the breakup experience facilitates post-breakup recovery and healing.

In a recent development, note: This content is only for informational and educational purposes and should not be considered therapy or any form of treatment. I cannot respond to personal requests for advice over the internet. Best on your continued journey.

The 10 Best Smartwatches for Men, Tested by Gear Editors

📅 31 Jul 2020 | ⏱️ 27 min read (5363 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~27 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AT MEN'S HEALTH, we love a good fitness tracker—but let’s be honest, they’re not exactly stylish.
  • With the Galaxy Watch9, Samsung didn’t mess with a good thing.
  • According to recent reports, one of the most notable new additions is the Vitals tool, which learns your normal range for things like heart rate and blood oxygen, then flags you when something’s off.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AT MEN'S HEALTH, we love a good fitness tracker—but let’s be honest, they’re not exactly stylish. Most of them look great with running shorts and a workout tee—but less so when you’re in a crisp dress shirt and tailored trousers. That’s where the best smartwatches for men come in. They bridge the gap between performance tech and actual style—tracking your heart rate and steps without clashing with your fit. A great smartwatch can go from your 6 a.m. run to your 8 p.m. cocktail hour without missing a beat. Some, like the TAG Heuer Connected, look so sleek you could wear them for a black-tie event and look like you belong on the cover of a magazine. We’ve tested dozens to find the ones that deliver that perfect balance of design, durability, and data.

With the Galaxy Watch9, Samsung didn’t mess with a good thing. The aluminum case, “squircle” shape, and bright 3,000-nit screen all carry over from the Watch8 that was our previous favorite—so at a glance you’d be hard-pressed to tell them apart. The key changes are under the hood: a bigger battery, a more power-efficient processor, and a smarter set of health tools that turn your sleep and workout data into advice you can act on.

According to recent reports, one of the most notable new additions is the Vitals tool, which learns your normal range for things like heart rate and blood oxygen, then flags you when something’s off. A jump in your resting heart rate or skin temperature, for instance, can signal a cold before you feel it—keep in mind these should be anecdotal. The other new features are for the data-driven crowd. A Heart Health Score rolls your sleep, activity, and blood-pressure trends into a single read on how your lifestyle is affecting your heart, with tips to improve it. My sleep schedule has been all over the place lately, making me feel lethargic at certain parts of the day, and the Watch9 has been recommending I go to bed earlier. Finally, a Fitness Index charts your body composition, cardio, endurance, flexibility, and strength on a spider graph so you can see where you’re strong and where you’re lagging.

There are carryovers from the Watch8 too, including the Running Coach that builds a plan off a 12-minute test run, with well-structured workouts, and the Antioxidant Index, which reads the carotenoid levels in your skin for a rough sense of your fruit and vegetable intake (to be taken with a grain of salt).

In a brief head-to-head test against the Apple Watch Series 11, the Watch9’s heart rate held within a few beats on runs and walks. I’ve been following a Couch to 5K program for the past four weeks, and the heart-rate readings during each run are reliable enough to pace by. Daily Cardio Load has also been a massive help, nudging me to dial it back instead of pushing myself too hard, too soon.

Samsung dropped the older Exynos chip for Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Wear Elite, and everything feels snappier, from starting a workout to pulling up a stat mid-run to talking to Google’s Gemini. Now you just lift your wrist to say a command, rather than first saying a wake word.

The Watch9 keeps the excellent Dynamic Lug System, making it comfortable enough to sleep in, and its premium-yet-friendly design moves from a morning run to a business-casual meeting without looking out of place. It comes in 40mm and 44mm sizes with a wider band lineup, including Sport, Fabric, and a two-tone Misty. The battery is bigger on paper—390mAh on the 40mm, a 20 percent bump, and in my testing it still lands around a day of use. At $379.99, Samsung’s newest model costs a bit more than the Watch8 did at launch, but you’re getting the smartest, most feature-packed version yet.

Read More: Best Fitness Trackers for Men.

It has been revealed that the Apple Watch SE used to be the Apple Watch you bought because you couldn’t justify spending more. Apple changed that with the SE 3 by adding an always-on display, the S10 chip, double-tap and wrist-flick gestures, 5G cellular on cellular models, and health features like Sleep Score and breathing irregularity detection through the Vitals app.

Over several weeks of testing, the SE 3 held up as a daily driver without feeling like a compromise. The always-on display made a real difference while exercising, and performance felt snappy across the board—from launching workouts to setting timers with on-device Siri. Fast charging is the other underrated upgrade. A 15-minute top-up while showering in the morning was enough to carry the watch through the rest of the day and overnight for sleep tracking.

After a rough night (67 out of 100), I could see exactly how that Sleep Score was calculated and adjusted accordingly, scoring a 90 the next night. The Vitals app runs in the background and tracks wrist temperature and respiratory rate without any input. It hasn’t flagged anything yet, but that kind of passive monitoring adds value over time.

Recent findings suggest that the newly introduced Series 12 is also available at $399. For the extra $150, it adds an ECG app, a Blood Oxygen app, and hypertension notifications, none of which the SE 3 has. It also takes a background heart rate reading every five seconds, and its Readiness app turns recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep into a single score.

The Series 12’s display reaches 2,000 nits (the SE 3 gets to 1,000), the bezels are thinner, and the screen area is larger. Battery life is rated at 24 hours compared to the SE 3’s 18 hours, and five minutes on the charger gives up to 10 hours of sleep tracking, where the SE 3 gets up to eight hours from eight minutes. The Series 12 also adds a water temperature sensor and a depth gauge to six meters for snorkeling.

It has been revealed that we recommend the Series 12 if you use a watch to follow training load and recovery, if you swim or snorkel, or if you want more advanced health tracking features. But the SE 3 is the call if you want notifications and standard workout and sleep tracking on an Apple Watch that still has an always-on display, and you’re on more of a budget.

Read More: Apple Watch SE 3 Review.

Sources indicate that if you want a GPS running watch that nails the fundamentals and is relatively affordable, the Coros Pace 4 should be at the top of your list. At $249, it competes on accuracy, battery life, and display quality with watches that cost significantly more, and at 40 grams with a silicone strap, it’s light enough to forget you’re wearing it.

In a recent development, the biggest upgrade from the Pace 3 is the AMOLED display, which is sharp and easy to read in bright sunlight. Battery life actually improved despite the brighter screen, jumping to 31 hours in max GPS mode with all satellite systems active, or 24 hours with always-on display enabled. A quick charge while you’re showering or eating a meal should top it off.

GPS tracking is where Coros built its reputation, and the Pace 4 delivers. Dual-frequency satellite support promises clean, accurate tracks that hold up even alongside buildings and under tree cover. The Pace 4 also features voice logging, so after finishing a run, the watch prompts you to record your thoughts, which get transcribed and saved in the Coros app. The watch also uses breadcrumb navigation rather than full maps, so if you rely on turn-by-turn directions while exploring fresh routes, you’ll want to step up to the Coros Apex or a Garmin with offline maps.

Read More: The Gear I Used to Train for My Longest Race Yet.

Our contributing editor and watch expert Ted Stafford, who styles every Men’s Health cover, was seriously impressed by the TAG Heuer Connected Calibre E5. “I was impressed by how well the E5 straddles the line between traditional style and modern innovation,” he says. “It wears beautifully on the wrist, with a sleek, stylish design and a comfort-first build. Its intuitive interface also makes it refreshingly simple to navigate, even on the move or during high-intensity activities.”.

Recent findings suggest that in fact, Stafford recently met with Tag Heuer’s team in Boston to test the Connected Calibre E5. During his 5K run, he appreciated how easy it was to glance at messages, check his heart rate, and accurately track his activity—all without slowing down. He also noted that the stainless bracelet stayed comfortable and secure the whole time. Another standout feature is the ability to customize the watch face. “Whether you’re in the mood for a sporty Carrera or a bold Formula 1 look, the E5 lets you effortlessly switch styles to match your day,” he indicates. “This and all the other unique tech offerings make having a connected watch a win-win for me.”.

What really makes the E5 shine, though, is how much it packs under the hood. You get dual-band GPS for pinpoint tracking, heart-rate and blood-oxygen sensors, and full sleep and stress tracking that rivals top fitness-focused wearables. The latest TAG Heuer OS runs smoother than ever, with cleaner visuals and tighter iPhone integration for those in the Apple ecosystem. Plus, it’s built like a tank with 50 meters of water resistance, a sapphire crystal display, and your choice of steel or titanium cases. Battery life clocks in at about two days of regular use, and fast charging gets you back to full in around 30 minutes.

It has been revealed that the Apple Watch Ultra 4 keeps the 49mm titanium case of the Ultra 3 and replaces the sensor on the back. The latest Health Sensing System adds a circular optical sensing array, larger and more efficient LEDs for heart rate readings, and more surface area touching the skin for ECG readings. Earlier models took background heart rate readings every five minutes. The Ultra 4 takes one every five seconds and demonstrates it in a new heart rate complication, which is a data point you pin to the watch face. Faster readings also let the watch measure heart rate variability (the variation in time between heartbeats) as often as every five minutes while you’re at rest.

The Ultra 4 also adds Readiness, which combines Fitness, Vitals, and Sleep Score into a rating from 1 to 10 for how prepared your body is for the day. Readiness needs several consecutive nights of sleeping with the watch before it starts scoring. The S11 chip makes the watch feel quicker and powers a upcoming step counter and better Siri, which our tester used to set timers more often than ever.

Apple rates the battery at up to 50 hours of normal use and up to 84 hours in Low Power Mode, with up to 18 hours of continuous workout tracking. In testing, the first charge lasted two nights of sleep. When the battery dropped to about 10 percent one night, our tester was almost three-quarters charged by the time he had brushed his teeth, gotten into bed, and set an alarm. Apple says 15 minutes on the charger gives up to 18 hours of use. Adventure watches from other brands can last weeks between charges, so the Ultra 4 still trails them.

The Ultra 4 costs $799 and the Series 12 costs $399. Both have the same sensors and health features, so the Ultra 4’s advantages are the bigger battery, the 49mm case, and adventure features like precision dual-frequency GPS, emergency SOS via satellite, and diving to 40 meters.

Read More: Apple Watch Ultra 4 Review.

When it comes to premium running watches, the latest Suunto Race (the Race 2) packs a serious punch at $499—or $599 for the Titanium Trail version. The display is larger and brighter than the Race 1 while being thinner. That mentioned, at 49mm, the Race 2 isn’t a small watch. Men’s Health Senior Gear and Reviews Editor Ryan Brower put it to the test, noting: “While I’ve enjoyed testing it, the Race 2 would be nice to have in a smaller size.”.

Recent findings suggest that that bigger size, though, makes room for a faster processor and an impressive 55 hours of battery life in GPS mode (or up to 30 days with daily use and no training). “The battery claims really hold,” Brower notes. “I’ve only had to charge it a couple of times throughout months of testing. To be fair, I don’t wear it every day, but I did for a few stretches to get a sense of it.” Another substantial improvement is the redesigned charging clip, which Brower found far more effective and reliable than previous Suunto models that didn’t always connect easily.

Performance-wise, the Race 2 delivers more than 115 sport modes. Brower put many of those programs through their paces—treadmill running, running, trail running, strength training, hiking, climbing, rowing (technically paddling), and even surfing—and each one worked smoothly, serving up plenty of useful metrics. GPS tracking proved fairly accurate, and features like training load and recovery provided deeper insights when synced with the Suunto Coach or other training apps. Building a regimen and letting the watch help implement it, Brower indicates, “can be a great tool for runners.”.

Sources indicate that the Race 2 leans into a rugged aesthetic with its large round case and durable polymer or titanium build. Its style clearly favors sport and outdoor fits, so the 49mm case can feel oversized or out of place in formal or office clothes. The standard strap is a breathable silicone, perfect for sweaty workouts or trail runs, and the Titanium Trail model adds a premium case finish for those who want a more elevated look in casual settings.

Read More: Garmin Vs. Apple Watch.

The Pixel Watch 5 looks almost identical to the Pixel Watch 4. It comes in the same 41mm and 45mm sizes, with a domed Actua 360 display under scratch-resistant Gorilla Glass that reaches 3,000 nits at its brightest. Most of the changes are inside and in the software. Google notes the new watch is 20 percent faster than the Pixel Watch 4, and it’s built around Gemini. Raise your wrist to talk to the assistant, and the watch face brings up things like flight info and your ETA when you need them.

Recent findings suggest that the Pixel Watch 5 can detect a loss of pulse and prompt a call to emergency services. Satellite SOS lets you contact emergency services and patch family from remote areas without cell service, and Google includes it free for two years after activation. Fall Detection, Car Crash Detection, and Safety Check are back, too. Safety Check shares your location with emergency contacts if a timer runs out during a solo run or a late walk home and you don’t respond.

According to recent reports, newly introduced this generation, the Pixel Watch 5 can show your blood pressure trends and track signs of insulin resistance over the course of a month. Google is clear that neither is a medical reading or a diagnosis, but both can flag patterns to bring up with your doctor. You also get the ECG app, irregular heart rhythm alerts, SpO2, HRV, skin temperature, and a nightly Sleep Score from what Google calls its most accurate sleep tracking yet. Each morning, Morning Brief combines your sleep recap, readiness, and the weather on one screen.

It has been revealed that google calls the watch’s dual-frequency GPS its best yet. It uses machine learning to keep runs through tall downtown buildings and hikes under thick tree cover on track. The watch tracks more than 50 activities. You can build strength sessions with exact reps, weights, and rest timers, and get audio and visual guidance as you go. A Google Health Premium subscription, which includes three free months, adds a Gemini-powered coach that adjusts your proposal around your schedule.

Recent findings suggest that google rates the battery at up to 30 hours for the 41mm model and up to 40 hours for the 45mm. That means charging most days, but the included Quick Charge Dock adds 15 hours in 15 minutes, so a short top-up in the morning gets you through a night of sleep tracking. The watch only works with Android phones, and at $399.99, it costs $50 more than the Pixel Watch 4 did at launch. If you’re an Android user who wants the strongest safety features on any smartwatch, it’s still the one to beat.

It has been revealed that the Fēnix 9 is Garmin’s premium multisport GPS watch, built for people who take their training and outdoor adventures seriously. It comes in 43mm, 47mm, and 51mm cases, with the 43mm model being styled for smaller wrists. Every version has an AMOLED display with a titanium bezel and a scratch-resistant sapphire lens, and it offers a much brighter screen than the Fēnix 8’s. The watch is tested to U.S. military standards for heat, shock, and water resistance, and it’s rated for recreational dives to 40 meters.

Navigation has always been Garmin’s forte, and it’s where the latest model stands apart. Full-color topographic maps come preloaded, and the Fēnix 9 has twice the RAM of the Fēnix 8 and an updated map engine that pans 30 percent faster. Storage doubles to 64GB, which holds twice as many maps as before plus up to 7,000 songs from Spotify, Deezer, or Amazon Music. Tell the watch how far you want to go, and dynamic round-trip routing suggests a loop that brings you back. If you go off course, it maps a fresh route with the same mileage. NextFork reveals the distance to the next trail junction and the name of the trail, ClimbPro shows current and upcoming climbs on downloaded courses, and SatIQ adjusts GPS accuracy to save battery.

Garmin rates the 43mm model at up to 10 days in smartwatch mode. That's a different category from any Apple Watch or Samsung Galaxy Watch, and it means far less battery anxiety day to day. You don’t have to be quite as strategic when you charge as you would with other smartwatches.

Industry observers note that the training tools go deeper than ever before, too. New stamina features show how your endurance holds up over different distances and help you manage your effort during a race. Garmin Epic combines several days of activities into one summary in the Garmin Connect app, which is useful for a backpacking trip or a training camp. Rowers get VO2 max and power metrics, and rucking workouts let you enter your pack weight.

In a recent development, returning features include Training Readiness, which scores your sleep, recovery, and training load each morning, along with HRV status, sleep coaching, PacePro race pacing, and an ECG app. A built-in speaker and microphone let you take calls from your wrist when the watch is paired with your iPhone or Android phone, and there's a built-in LED flashlight.

The 43mm Fēnix 9 is pricey at $999.99, and more advanced connectivity features like inReach satellite messaging, SOS, and LTE calling require the more expensive Fēnix 9 Pro, so the standard model relies on your paired phone to send your live location if it detects an incident. But for athletes who log serious miles across multiple sports and want one watch that handles all of it, the Fēnix 9 is the way to go.

Recent findings suggest that we got our hands on the G-Shock Move, and this thing is a beast—in the best way possible. Built with G-Shock’s signature toughness, it feels indestructible yet surprisingly comfortable on the wrist. I ran, lifted, and hiked with it, and it handled everything without a hiccup. Inside, you’ve got serious hardware: GPS, heart-rate monitoring, altimeter, compass, thermometer, and a gyroscope that tracks every stride, step, and elevation change with precision.

According to recent reports, what really impressed me was how capable it felt in different conditions. I tracked a few long runs with GPS fully active, and the data stayed consistent and accurate the whole time—no weird pace spikes or drop-offs. The battery life held up too; even when I pushed it hard, I still got several days before needing a recharge. And when it does run low, the solar-assisted charging converts sunlight into extra power, adding several hours—or even a day or two—of runtime if you’re outdoors. It’s rated for 200 meters of water resistance, so swimming, rain, and sweat are all fair game.

Sources indicate that living up to its name, the G-Shock Move supports more than a dozen sports, from trail running and cycling to gym training and open-water swimming, while also monitoring sleep, recovery, and blood-oxygen levels. The display’s bright and easy-to-read mid-workout, and the interface feels intuitive enough to switch modes on the fly. For guys who demand a watch that’s as tough and versatile as they are, this one’s the real deal.

The Fitbit Edge is a fitness tracker first, with just enough smartwatch features to cover the basics. You can read notifications, send quick replies, set alarms, control your music, get turn-by-turn directions from Google Maps, and find your phone. But there are no calls, no contactless payments, no voice assistant, and no app store.

In a recent development, that limited feature set is why the battery lasts up to seven days and charges back to full in 90 minutes. The rounded display is also 45 percent bigger and more than 40 percent brighter than on previous Fitbits, and it shows your stats and coaching cues at a glance.

Built-in GPS and an altimeter let you map outdoor runs, rides, and hikes and track how much you climb without bringing your phone. The Edge also recognizes workouts automatically, so a walk or run still counts if you forget to start it. The tracker records heart rate, HRV, SpO2, breathing rate, skin temperature, and resting heart rate. Each night it also tracks your sleep stages and gives you a Sleep Score. High and low heart rate alerts and Irregular Rhythm Notifications flag potential heart issues.

It has been revealed that A Google Health Premium membership, which comes with three free months and then costs $9.99 a month, unlocks a Gemini-powered coach that builds a training plan around your schedule. It also adds blood pressure and insulin resistance trends. Google claims neither is a clinical reading nor a screening tool, but both can flag patterns to discuss with your doctor.

According to recent reports, at $179.99, the Edge works with both iPhone and Android phones and comes with small and large bands in the box. It’s a good fit if a full smartwatch is more than you need but you still want to see texts and directions on your wrist. If you want calls, payments, and apps, look at the Pixel Watch 5 or Apple Watch SE 3 instead.

Read More: Google Fitbit Air Vs. Fitbit Edge.

According to recent reports, yes, but how much they can do depends on whether the watch has cellular. Any watch with built-in GPS can track workouts, heart rate, and sleep without your phone. Some, like the Garmin Fēnix 9, also store maps and music so you can navigate and listen on a phone-free run.

For texts, calls, and notifications, you need a cellular model. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 comes with cellular built in, while the Apple Watch SE 3 and Series 12 offer it as an upgrade. Watches without cellular, along with fitness trackers like the Fitbit Edge, stop getting notifications once you're out of range of your phone. Some options like the Ultra 4 also add satellite SOS, which lets you reach emergency services when there's no cell service at all.

It has been revealed that smartwatches are more accurate than ever, thanks to newer optical sensors, more LEDs, and more sensor area touching your skin. Most of today’s flagship watches from Apple, Google, Samsung, and Garmin are reliable enough for everyday tracking and most workouts. A chest strap is still the most precise option, though, so pair one with your watch for hard intervals or races. The Garmin Fēnix 9, for example, works with Garmin's HRM 600. Over time, trends in your heart rate are more useful than any single reading, so wear your watch consistently.

Most full-featured smartwatches last one to two days on a charge, while fitness-focused watches can go a week or more. The Google Pixel Watch 5 is rated at up to 30 hours for the 41mm model and up to 40 hours for the 45mm, and the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is rated at up to 50 hours (up to 84 hours in low power mode). Garmin rates the 43mm Fēnix 9 at up to 10 days, the Fitbit Edge lasts up to seven, and the Suunto Race 2 can go up to 30 days with daily use when you’re not tracking workouts.

Your actual battery life depends on how you use the watch, since GPS tracking, continuous heart rate monitoring, and an always-on display all drain it faster. If you track your sleep, look for fast charging, too. Apple says 15 minutes on the charger gives the Ultra 4 up to 18 hours of use, and 15 minutes on Google’s Quick Charge Dock adds 15 hours to the Pixel Watch 5.

Fabric and silicone bands are best for workouts because they’re lightweight, breathable, and dry quickly. Woven nylon and elastic straps adjust easily and won’t dig into your wrist mid-run, though they can hold onto odor and need an occasional wash. Metal bracelets in stainless steel, titanium, or aluminum give a smartwatch a polished, traditional look for the office or a formal event, but they feel heavy during workouts and can trap sweat. Leather bands dress up a watch for work or dinner and mold to your wrist over time. They’re not a great option for workouts, though, because sweat and water can warp or stain them.

Sources indicate that A lifestyle or hybrid smartwatch is the best fit for most offices, because it’s sleek enough for business casual and still tough enough for the gym. The Samsung Galaxy Watch9 is a good example, with a slim aluminum case that works with casual, sporty, and business-casual outfits. If you dress up more often, a luxury smartwatch like the TAG Heuer Connected Calibre E5 pairs a stainless steel case and sapphire crystal with performance tracking, and it looks right with a suit. Adventure watches like the Suunto Race 2 and Garmin Fēnix 9 have larger cases built for trail running, hiking, and multisport training, while rugged watches like the Casio G-Shock Move are shock- and water-resistant for tough conditions. Both are better suited to the weekend than a client meeting.

According to recent reports, every smartwatch should handle notifications, music controls, and heart rate and sleep tracking. Built-in GPS is worth having if you run, ride, or hike without your phone. Beyond the basics, the features worth paying for depend on how you train. Runners and outdoor athletes should look for dual-frequency GPS and offline maps, like those on the Garmin Fēnix 9 and Suunto Race 2. If you want guidance, look for training intends that adapt to your progress, like Garmin Coach or the Gemini-powered coach in Google Health Premium. For recovery, look for HRV, sleep scores, and readiness scores, which the Apple Watch Ultra 4, Pixel Watch 5, and Fēnix 9 all offer. If you want to leave your phone at home, look for an onboard voice assistant like Siri or Gemini, contactless payments, and LTE for calls and texts.

Bracelets (or metal bands) are best for work, formal occasions, and everyday wear. They give your smartwatch a more polished, traditional-watch look—great for dressing up or blending your tech into a sleek outfit. Stainless steel feels classic and weighty, while titanium offers a lighter, more premium feel with added durability. Aluminum links are affordable and comfortable for all-day wear. However, metal can feel heavy during workouts and may trap sweat, so they’re better for the office than the gym.

Fabric bands are great for casual wear, fitness tracking, and comfort-first users. The straps are lightweight, breathable, and soft against the skin, making them great for long wear or sweaty workouts. Woven nylon or elastic options adjust easily, dry quickly, and don’t dig into your wrist mid-run. Fabric bands can hold onto odor or discolor over time, so they’ll need a wash if you’re wearing them to the gym often.

Leather bands work for everyday and office wear, and dressed-up casual looks. This material instantly elevates a smartwatch—ideal if you want tech that doesn’t scream “tech.” A good leather strap molds to your wrist over time and works seamlessly from the office to dinner. However, leather doesn’t love sweat or water, so it can warp or stain after a tough workout or shower.

According to recent reports, to pick the best smartwatches, we didn’t just look at specs—we constantly put them to the test in real life. Our contributing editor and watch expert Ted Stafford, who styles every Men’s Health cover shoot, weighed in on how they feel on the wrist and how versatile they are for everyday wear. Ryan Brower, our Senior Gear and Reviews Editor, tested the watches’ performance, accuracy, and tech features over weeks of workouts and training sessions. Our fitness editors logged miles, tracked recovery, monitored sleep, and pushed each watch through tough workouts to see which ones could actually keep up. After combining all their hands-on notes, we narrowed the list to the models that deliver on style, durability, comfort, battery life, smart features, and reliable health and fitness tracking.

Smartwatches won't replace your smartphone, but they can be a great complementary accessory. Most of today's smartwatches can provide alerts for calls, texts, emails, calendar notifications, and more. The best smartwatches also add outdoor-centric features like GPS-enabled maps with route-tracking. Plus, many people like smartwatches for advanced health and fitness tracking, as many premium options can monitor sleep patterns, track stress levels and heart rate throughout the day, and even provide accident or emergency warnings (as with Apple's Crash Detection feature).

Depending on the make and model, most smartwatches last about two to four years—but it's entirely possible for yours to last longer or much shorter depending on use. Today's models are durable enough to handle years of daily wear, so longevity isn't usually the matter. What tends to make your smartwatch feel outdated is old software that can't keep up with the latest updates or app integrations.

According to recent reports, if you wear your smartwatch every day and rely on it for calls, texts, and fitness tracking, you'll likely want to upgrade every couple of years to stay current with the newest software and performance features. If you wear your smartwatch a couple of days a week or just for fitness purposes, then you'll be okay with sticking to the watch you have for a longer period of time. After all, you're still getting the same high-quality performance tracking metrics regardless of the software you're running.

*Additional reporting by Joseph Cheatham.

Latest Update: Pearley: How the Saab 99 Turbo Changed the World

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1204 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, it didn’t seem so at the time, but 1977 would prove to be among the most important years in automotive history.
  • Industry observers note that yeah, Saab isn’t around today; there were turbocharged cars built before it; and the 99 never sold in overwhelming numbers (at least not here in America).
  • In a recent development, the 99 was already ancient by 1977.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it didn’t seem so at the time, but 1977 would prove to be among the most important years in automotive history. Commercially, this was the model year when General Motors “downsized” its full-size cars from gargantuan to merely huge. Their immense sales success meant the era of land dreadnoughts was over. It was the first model year for the BMW 3-Series name in America and the first for the Porsche 924, that company’s first front-engine car. In Formula One, Colin Chapman introduced ground effects aerodynamics to the series with the revolutionary Lotus 78. Culturally, 1977 was the year of Smokey and the Bandit, which continues to define what a silly car chase movie must be. But quite sneakily, with 50 years of hindsight, the most important development of 1977 was the introduction of the Saab 99 Turbo.

Industry observers note that yeah, Saab isn’t around today; there were turbocharged cars built before it; and the 99 never sold in overwhelming numbers (at least not here in America). But almost every car for sale today derives at least some of its essence from that eccentric Swedish front-driver. “Saab’s use of a turbocharger differs considerably from that of other car makers, such as Porsche,” reported John Lamm in Road & Track’s October 1977 road test. “[I]n that Saab’s goal is maximum torque at mid-range engine speeds rather than dramatic boost at high output.”.

In a recent development, the 99 was already ancient by 1977. Originally shown in 1967 as Saab’s first stretch beyond dinky cars with weird two-stroke engines, it went into production in 1968 as a 1969 model and was, by Saab’s standards, a hit. But it was still weird—wraparound windshield, odd ducky styling, and yeah, the ignition key was down behind the shifter—and at a time when front-wheel drive was rare, it was front-drive.

In a recent development, saab’s buyers had a certain academic and liberal edge, too. According to researchers at the University of Connecticut and reported by Time magazine in 1976, a staggering 98 percent of Saab owners voted for Democratic candidate George McGovern over Republican incumbent Richard Nixon in the 1972 presidential election. In that election, Nixon carried 60.7 percent of the vote, and won 49 of the 50 states. Saab owners weren’t like everyone else.

Sources indicate that the 99’s “Slant-4” four-cylinder engine was based on the V-8 installed in the British Triumph Stag. By 1972, Saab had taken over production of the engine itself, and had modified the design to be robust and reliable, but there was nothing exotic about what Saab now called the B engine. It had an iron block and a single overhead cam aluminum head. Simple stuff. And in the 1976 99 EMS, the sportiest model in the line, the 2.0-liter eight-valve engine was rated at 115 horsepower channeled through a four-speed manual transmission.

Saab didn’t have the resources to develop a newly introduced engine, but it had plenty of turbocharging experience with its Scania large truck division. “The immediate problem,” explained R&T’s Thos. L. Bryant after driving the new 99 Turbo in Sweden for the December 1976 matter, “was to get low-speed torque for the drivability while at the same time limiting high engine speed power for durability.” To achieve that goal, Saab used small turbochargers and advanced electronic engine controls.

Saab already used Bosch K-Jetronic fuel injection on the B engine, and while it wasn’t a wholly electronic system, it was good at advanced fuel metering. And it was the same system Porsche used on the 911 Turbo. Also, Saab developed its own electronic Automatic Performance Control (APC) that used a knock sensor in the block and pressure sensors in the intake manifold to trigger a wastegate and limit turbo boost when the engine couldn’t take any more.

Sources indicate that saab didn’t hide the small, quick-spooling Garrett T3 turbocharger in the 99, putting it forward of the engine. And what was downstream of it was nearly as important. Saab breakthrough emissions tech, known as “Lambda,” ensured that performance could be compatible with stricter emissions controls and catalytic converters. “Basically, Lambda is a 3-component catalyst designed to handle NOx as well as CO and HC,” explained Bryant. “The normal catalytic converter takes care of the last two pollutants fairly well, but NOx usually requires lower compression ratios and exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) to keep it from being passed out through the tailpipe.”.

Lambda added three pieces alongside the fuel injection system: There was an oxygen sensor to monitor air-fuel mixture; an electronic control system that tweaked the air-fuel mixture to keep it close to the ideal stoichiometric value; and a switch on the throttle housing to override the metering system under full-load conditions. It was effective enough so that the engine could meet California’s 1977 emissions without using an Exhaust Gas Recirculation (EGR) valve.

It has been revealed that altogether, those elements and many subtler tweaks meant the 99 Turbo had 135 horsepower aboard. Not a lot by 2026 standards, but a sweet chunk back then. “In all of our discussions about the Saab Turbo,” R&T reported in the October 1977 test, “the one comment that continually surfaced was. ‘It’s so much fun to drive!’ Obviously, with a net horsepower rating up 20 hp to 135 at 5000 rpm (net torque is 160 at 3500 rpm versus 123 lb-ft for the non-turbocharged Saab and that is the more revealing improvement), the Saab Turbo is not going to give the breathtaking acceleration of a Porsche Turbo Carrera, but the performance increase is substantial and worthwhile.” R&T measured the 99 Turbo waltzing to 60 mph in 9.5 seconds, and running the quarter-mile in 17.5 seconds at 80.5 mph. In the context of the time, a solid performance.

Sources indicate that the 99 Turbo wasn’t perfect, but showcased how effective turbocharging and electronic engine controls could be. At the same moment GM was using dumb carburetors on its fresh 1977 turbocharged Buick V-6, Saab was showing how it could be done. Buick would eventually adopt fuel injection and better electronic engine controls to allow its blown V-6 to mature into a legend with the Grand National and GNX. But Saab was there first.Saab died a sad death after some corporate conniptions. But look around at the turbocharged engines that dominate today. All those engines, powering everything from the Honda Civic Type R to the Kia Telluride, are descendants of the Saab 99 Turbo, which went on sale 50 years ago. As one anonymous staff member noted in that first road test, “This to me is one of the waves of the future: small engine with turbocharger for fuel economy and performance coupled with low exhaust emissions. Neat!”.

In a recent development, john Pearley Huffman has been writing about cars since 1990 and is getting okay at it. Besides Road & Track, his work has appeared in Car and Driver, the New York Times, and more than 100 automotive publications and websites. A graduate of UC Santa Barbara, he still lives near that campus with his wife and two children. He owns a pair of Toyota Tundras and two dogs. He used to have a Nova and a Camaro.

Potatoes grown in moon dirt are as nutritious as Earth potatoes

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (573 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronauts living in the first permanent lunar base may see a sizable number of spuds on their dinner plates.
  • Industry observers note that “We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter,” Aymeric Goyer, an OSU botanist and study co-author, stated in a statement.
  • Recent findings suggest that even in a controlled habitat, life on the moon will be physically demanding for astronauts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronauts living in the first permanent lunar base may see a sizable number of spuds on their dinner plates. In a study published today in the journal npj Microgravity, botanists at Oregon State University (OSU) proved it’s possible to grow healthy, edible potatoes in simulated moon soil with the help of everyday worms. Importantly, the team also identified the proper proportions of lunar regolith and compost needed to produce potato yields similar to those grown on Earth.

Industry observers note that “We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter,” Aymeric Goyer, an OSU botanist and study co-author, stated in a statement. “That’s an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the Moon.”.

Recent findings suggest that even in a controlled habitat, life on the moon will be physically demanding for astronauts. They’ll require carefully maintained, nutritious diets to keep them healthy, but it’s not as simple as sending them off packed with calorically dense prepackaged meals. Cargo room on spacecraft is limited and costly, and the desolate lunar surface isn’t exactly hospitable to agriculture. In addition to constant bombardment by cosmic and solar radiation, temperatures can swing anywhere between 250 degrees and -410 degrees Fahrenheit.

According to recent reports, indoor horticulture will also be challenging. Lunar regolith is an annoyingly powdery substance composed of sharp-edged, miniscule particles created over billions of years of asteroid impacts, but little else. With essentially no organic material at all, the dust alone isn’t capable of supporting plant life.

While it is easy enough to combine that lunar regolith with agricultural additives, researchers weren’t sure if these could overcome moon soil’s heavy metals and irradiation. To test it, Goyer and his colleagues first obtained simulated lunar regolith made to resemble the samples collected during the Apollo missions. Regolith composition varies by region on the moon, so they selected five different types based on darker lunar mare dust and the lighter lunar highland soil. They then mixed the mock moon dust with vermicompost, the nutrient-rich soil created when worms break down organic materials. Next, they planted potatoes in various ratios of regolith and vermicompost, and monitored their growth. As a control, the team even planted potatoes in soil taken from Hermiston, Oregon, an area famous for some of the world’s highest spud yields.

The team found that composite soil with only 30 percent vermicompost was enough to produce potato crops comparable to those farmed on Earth. Their findings suggest the supplemental organics bind to the regolith’s heavy metals, which shield the plants and minimize any damage to their roots.

“We believe the compost helps balance some of the toxicity we see in lunar regolith,” added OSU botanist and study co-author David Handy.

Industry observers note that but bushels of moon potatoes only go so far if they lack any real nutritional value. Even here, the lunar simulations offered promising results, particularly when it came to glycoalkaloids. The naturally forming potato toxins can cause green skin discoloration, but analysis indicated no statistically relevant rise in glycoalkaloids for the lunar crops.

With the potato viability debate settled, Goyer’s team will next compare 10 specific spud varieties grown in simulated lunar regolith to determine the most nutritious and resilient options for NASA astronomers.

#75666. Muscle Size vs. Strength: Which Matters More for Living Longer? Experts Explain

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1759 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Womenshealthmag ↗ Open Full Page

Muscle Size vs. Strength: Which Matters More for Living Longer? Experts Explain

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1759 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When it comes to aging well, you've probably heard that building muscle is one of the best things you can do for your body.
  • Resistance training, which is often used as an umbrella term, can have different goals, including building muscle size and increasing maximal strength.
  • On the other hand, training for maximal strength focuses on improving how much force your muscles can produce.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When it comes to aging well, you've probably heard that building muscle is one of the best things you can do for your body. And it's true: Maintaining muscle mass is essential for staying healthy, mobile, and independent as you get older. But here's something you might not realize: Having more muscle doesn't necessarily mean you're stronger. And when it comes to living as long (and as well!) as possible, that distinction matters.

Resistance training, which is often used as an umbrella term, can have different goals, including building muscle size and increasing maximal strength. Training for muscle growth, known as hypertrophy training, focuses on increasing the size of your muscles, says Vonda Wright, MD, an orthopedic surgeon who researches longevity and muscle health.

On the other hand, training for maximal strength focuses on improving how much force your muscles can produce. It’s often measured by how much weight you can lift in a particular exercise, Dr. Wright explains. Although larger muscles have the potential to produce more force, muscle size alone doesn’t determine strength. “That’s why someone who is smaller can sometimes be stronger than someone with visibly larger muscles,” she adds.

Recent findings suggest that meet the experts: Vonda Wright, MD, is an orthopedic surgeon and author of Unbreakable. Mark Kovacs, PhD, CSCS, is an exercise physiologist, longevity and human performance specialist, and founder of the Kovacs Institute in Atlanta. Stuart Phillips, PhD, is a muscle researcher and professor of kinesiology at McMaster University. Ben Walker, CPT, is a personal trainer and founder of Anywhere Fitness in Dublin, Ireland.

According to recent reports, still, both adaptations play an notable role in healthy aging—especially since muscle mass and strength naturally decline with age. Building muscle supports your joints and bones, helps regulate metabolic health, and gives you the strength and physical capacity to keep moving and stay active, says Mark Kovacs, PhD, CSCS, an exercise physiologist, longevity and human performance specialist, and founder of the Kovacs Institute. Strength, meanwhile, allows you to put that muscle to work, whether you’re carrying groceries, climbing stairs, or getting up from the floor, he explains.

It’s imperative to build both strength and muscle for a long, healthy life. But if your goal is to stay active and independent well into your later years, one may be worth prioritizing over the other.

Resistance training can help you build muscle and become stronger, but these are distinct goals that emphasize different outcomes. Training for muscle growth focuses on increasing muscle size, while training for maximal strength focuses on improving how much force you can produce, claims Kovacs. The two goals overlap, and people typically gain both muscle and strength through resistance training. But you can formulate your workouts to emphasize one outcome over the other, he adds.

For instance, if your goal is maximal strength, the weight you lift matters more. So, training for strength means practicing movements with loads that feel heavy to you, says Stuart Phillips, PhD, a muscle researcher and professor of kinesiology at McMaster University. Strength gains depend not only on muscle size, but also on how effectively your nervous system activates your muscles and how efficiently you perform the movement. “Lighter weights can still make you stronger, but taking them to failure doesn’t automatically make them equivalent to heavier training for maximizing strength,” Phillips explains. For this goal, he recommends 2 to 3 sets of roughly 4 to 8 reps with a challenging weight, stopping before your technique breaks down.

Recent findings suggest that in terms of muscle growth, both lighter and heavier weights can build muscle—what matters is that your body is sufficiently challenged. Of course, lighter weights will require more repetitions to grow muscle, Phillips claims. (In fact, his research demonstrates that performing roughly 20 to 25 repetitions with light weights produced similar muscle growth to sets of 8 to 12 repetitions with heavier weights when both were taken to failure.).

According to recent reports, as a rule of thumb, Phillips recommends choosing a weight that makes the last few reps feel challenging while leaving about two good reps in reserve. (If you finish 25 reps and feel like you could easily do five more, the weight is probably too light to provide enough of a stimulus to spark growth.) One way to gauge this is with the resistance-training rating of perceived exertion (RPE) scale, which measures how hard a set feels based on how many more reps you think you could complete with good form, he explains. The scale runs from 1 to 10: An RPE of eight means you could squeeze out about two more reps, a 9 means you have one left, and a 10 means you’ve reached failure and can’t complete another rep.

According to recent reports, the number of sets you perform matters for building muscle, too. Doing one challenging set per exercise consistently over time can grow muscle, Phillips claims, but research suggests that performing multiple sets generally leads to greater muscle growth.

It has been revealed that strength, which is the maximum force you can produce in a particular task, directly influences how well you can move through everyday life. “Strong muscles support our skeleton, protect our joints, improve metabolic health, and allow us to continue doing the things we love at 50, 70, and 90,” indicates Dr. Wright. Strength helps us with getting up off the floor, carrying our own suitcase, climbing a mountain, playing with grandchildren, and living independently long-term.

Consider something as simple as getting out of a chair. When you’re younger and stronger, Kovacs states that movement may require only a small percentage of your maximum strength. As you lose strength with age, though, that same movement requires more of what you have available. If you aren’t regularly training it, everyday activities can become increasingly difficult, he explains. But when you continue to build strength as you age, you have more to pull from, making those activities easier.

It has been revealed that additionally, research draws a direct connection between strength and a longer life: A 2026 study in JAMA Network Open looked at the association between muscular strength and mortality. Over 5,000 women ages 63 to 99 underwent testing for grip strength, chair stand performance, and a timed walk test. Participants also mailed health update questionnaires annually between 2012 and 2014 until 2023. They found that higher muscle strength was associated with lower mortality.

It has been revealed that strength training is also associated with cardiometabolic benefits, endurance performance, and bone density—which are all crucial for living long and well. In fact, a small 2022 study in Sensors had 29 postmenopausal women with osteopenia or osteoporosis (when you have lower bone mineral density than normal) either do strength training exercises with heavy and moderately heavy weights, or no exercise at all, for six months. The group that strength trained had higher bone mineral density at the end of the trial period.

Muscle is one of your body’s best forms of insurance for getting older. Everyday activities depend on having enough muscle (as well as strength) to do them independently. “Muscle supports our joints and loads our bones, helping stimulate the bone-building process, but it’s also essential to mobility and functional strength," Dr. Wright explains. “If we want to continue getting ourselves off the ground, climbing stairs, carrying things, traveling, playing sports, and living independently, we need muscle to do it.”.

Research also concludes that less muscle mass is associated with a higher risk of mortality. A 2023 review in PLOS One observed 16 studies with over 81,000 participants and looked at the connection between their body composition and when they died. The review concluded that a low skeletal muscle mass index was significantly associated with an increased risk of all-cause mortality.

It has been revealed that additionally, having muscle mass can improve your metabolic health. A 2025 study in Nutrition & Metabolism had older participants with type 2 diabetes either build muscle through resistance training alone, resistance training and eating a whey protein supplement, or doing neither of the two, for 12 weeks. Those who completed the muscle-building interventions significantly improved their blood glucose control and insulin resistance.

Industry observers note that plus, lower muscle mass is linked to poor balance and a higher risk of falls. So, maintaining muscle helps protect your mobility and independence as you age, Dr. Wright adds. A 2020 study in Menopause Review had 122 women over 60 do physical performance tests (gait speed test, grip strength, and a timed up and go). Their body composition was measured, and they filled out a survey of how often they fell in the past year. Less muscle was associated with a higher risk of falls.

In a recent development, A well-rounded workout plan should naturally progress both muscular size and strength. After all, they address different pieces of the same puzzle and one form of training can help you make progress in the other. As you build muscle, you generally increase the amount of tissue available to produce force, says Ben Walker, CPT, a certified personal trainer and founder of Anywhere Fitness in Dublin, Ireland. And as you train for strength, your brain and nervous system become better at coordinating and activating those muscles, he explains.

In a recent development, if you’re looking for a initiative that’ll help you build both strength and muscle, check out our Women’s Health+ exclusive workout looks. Each one comes with four weeks of expert-programmed workouts, science-backed nutrition advice, and evidence-based recovery methods.

It has been revealed that remember, longevity isn’t about simply adding years to your life. It’s about extending your healthspan, or the number of years you remain healthy, mobile, and strong. “The goal is to bring our healthspan as close to our lifespan as possible, and for me, that means building a body that can carry you through the life you want to live,” says Dr. Wright. That way, you’ll be ready to throw grandkids around at 60, deadlift hundreds of pounds at 70, and lift your own suitcase on vacation with your family in your 80s and beyond.
