The Harm of Trying to Change Your Sexual Orientation

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1049 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.
  • When people hear “conversion therapy,” they may picture a teenager forced into treatment by parents or religious leaders.
  • According to recent reports, in March 2026, the Supreme Court ruled that a Colorado ban on conversion therapy may violate free speech rules.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.

When people hear “conversion therapy,” they may picture a teenager forced into treatment by parents or religious leaders. But efforts to change sexual orientation often begin privately: someone prays for their attractions to disappear, suppresses sexual thoughts, or avoids relationships in hopes of becoming heterosexual.

According to recent reports, in March 2026, the Supreme Court ruled that a Colorado ban on conversion therapy may violate free speech rules. Proponents of the ban argued that people who want to change their sexual orientation should be allowed to try. This raises an key question, answered by recent research—what happens when a person sincerely wants this change?

Industry observers note that A new study offers a troubling answer: self-initiated efforts to change sexual orientation were associated with greater depression, less social support, and greater disconnection from oneself—without evidence that they changed sexual orientation. Choosing to pursue change does not establish that the pursuit is safe or effective.

Recent findings suggest that psychologist G. Tyler Lefevor and colleagues followed current and former members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints over two years. Their study included 315 participants with information about change efforts at both assessments. Unlike research that asks people to reconstruct experiences years later, this study followed participants forward in time. The researchers also registered their research plan in advance and assembled a team with differing perspectives on sexual orientation change efforts. This is an notable way the researchers demonstrated commitment to objectivity and research ethics.

In a recent development, nearly three-quarters of participants reported trying to change their same-gender sexuality at some point. Forty-three reported ongoing or recently ended efforts at the beginning of the study.

Recent findings suggest that those participants were struggling more than people who were no longer trying or had never tried. They reported more depressive symptoms, lower well-being, poorer self-rated health, and less support from friends and family. They were also less open about their sexuality and more alienated from their own experiences.

Two years later, the group initially pursuing change still reported more depression and less support from friends. However, the overall test combining health outcomes was not statistically significant, and the researchers found no significant difference in suicidality. The depression difference averaged about two points on a commonly used questionnaire, with both groups’ averages falling within the mild range.

In a recent development, these findings deserve attention. This was an observational study, and participants were already experiencing distress when it began. It cannot establish whether change efforts caused depression, whether distress encouraged people to pursue change, or whether both reflected other pressures. Most participants were White adults from one religious background, and relatively few were actively pursuing change.

Nevertheless, the findings challenge the reassurance that personally desired change efforts are harmless and should be allowed.

Sources indicate that A person can sincerely choose something while carrying painful beliefs about what makes them acceptable. “I want to become straight” may coexist with “I am afraid I will lose my family,” “I cannot imagine belonging in my faith community as I am,” or “My attractions mean there is something wrong with me.”.

Recent findings suggest that this study did not establish that these change efforts were entirely free of outside influence. “Self-initiated” describes who undertakes the effort; it does not establish where the desire originated. Nor did it mean everyone worked alone: participants’ experiences could include personal practices, groups, or other assistance.

That distinction matters. An external demand can become an internal rule, enforced without anyone else in the room.

Recent findings suggest that one possible cost is persistent self-surveillance. Every attraction or sexual thought becomes something to monitor. Every unwanted erotic desire or impulse becomes evidence of failure. When attractions persist, a person may conclude that they have not prayed enough, worked hard enough, or shown sufficient commitment.

Sources indicate that another possible cost is isolation. Avoiding people who evoke attraction—or communities that offer acceptance—may reduce opportunities for friendship, intimacy, and honest conversation. The study’s findings of lower support and greater self-alienation fit these concerns, although they do not prove these particular pathways caused the distress.

Recent findings suggest that the promised benefit also failed to materialize in the study’s comparisons. Participants pursuing change showed no significantly different changes in same-gender or other-gender attraction, sexual aversion, or sexual behavior over two years. Nearly 63 percent of those initially classified as pursuing change were no longer doing so by follow-up, having given up trying to change their sexuality.

Sexuality can show natural variation over time. People can also change their behavior, relationships, or identity labels. None of those changes, by itself, demonstrates that an intervention can reliably turn same-gender attraction into heterosexuality.

Sources indicate that respecting personal autonomy remains essential. People deserve to make their own decisions about faith, relationships, sexual behavior, and the language they use for themselves. A therapist should not prescribe a particular identity or relationship.

But respecting someone’s choices also requires being honest about the evidence and helping them examine the costs of their goals. Someone seeking help can explore religious commitments, relationship decisions, grief, and fear without being promised that their attractions can be eliminated. Choosing celibacy or setting boundaries around behavior is a different goal from trying to change the attractions themselves. Sex therapist Jack Morin famously described that when people go to war with their own sexuality, they are likely to end up worse than they started.

The clinical task is to help people build a life they can inhabit with dignity, connection, and less self-rejection.

According to recent reports, A sincere desire to become heterosexual does not guarantee that pursuing that goal will help. This research adds to concerns that the pursuit can accompany continuing distress while delivering no demonstrated change in orientation. People experiencing that conflict deserve support that takes both their values and their well-being seriously.

Industry observers note that source: Lefevor, G. T., Rosik, C. H., Beckstead, A. L., Mansfield, T. R., & Yarhouse, M. A. (2026). A preregistered, prospective, longitudinal examination of the impact of self-initiated sexual orientation change efforts on health and changes in sexuality. Archives of Sexual Behavior.

Recent findings suggest that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

According to recent reports, if you work from home, you know how much of a difference the right office chair can make. Take it from someone who's spent five years working remotely and learned the hard way that the couch isn't the best place to spend a workday. Between a standing desk, an under-desk treadmill, and monitors, outfitting your home office can get expensive. But if you're going to splurge on one piece of WFH gear, an ergonomic office chair that supports your back throughout the workday is a good place to start.

“A supportive chair can reduce the risk of lower back pain, neck and upper back pain, poor circulation, and fatigue,” notes Kevin Lees, director of chiropractic operations at The Joint Chiropractic. “This may also lead to improved productivity, enabling individuals to stay focused on their tasks without distractions from trying to get comfortable.”.

According to recent reports, to find the best home office chairs, our team consulted spine specialists and tested several popular ergonomic chairs for weeks in our own workspaces, sitting for up to eight hours a day. Our favorite is the Branch Ergonomic Chair Pro, which impressed us with its customizable support and easy assembly at a reasonable price compared to premium models from Herman Miller and Steelcase.

The right home office chair will be different for everyone, but there are a lot of factors that will remain the same, like adjustable lumbar support and thick seat cushioning. Keep reading to find which of these eight expert-recommended chairs are the perfect addition to your workday.

Meet the experts: Kevin Lees, Director of Chiropractic Operations at The Joint Chiropractic.Dr. Gbolohan Okubadejo, a spine surgeon and the head of The Institute of Comprehensive Spine Care.

The Branch Ergonomic Chair Pro is our pick for the best home office chair because of its combination of comfort, adjustability, and value. At $499, it’s packed with easy-to-use adjustments that make it a steal. You can customize the seat depth, lumbar support, tilt tension, recline, and more without having to take your eyes away from your work.

It has been revealed that after testing the chair for over a month and sitting for four to six hours per workday, WH Digital Designer Taryn Colbert gave it a five out of five, praising how easy it was to assemble and customize. In fact, she found herself using it even when she wasn't working.

“While I work, I sit it up to work on my posture,” she says. When doing her hair or playing computer games, she reclines the chair into what she calls “lounge mode.”.

According to recent reports, the armrests alone offer five types of adjustment, and you can add a headrest or a taller cylinder for an additional cost. While the mesh version has a low-key look, the leather and vegan leather options are worth considering if you want a bit more style.

Colbert’s biggest gripe was the wide wheelbase, which made it difficult to maneuver through doorways and across carpet.

Still, if you’re looking for a classic ergonomic office chair, this model is great for both first-timers and seasoned remote workers. Its customizable design is intuitive enough to use every day without requiring a four-figure investment.

According to recent reports, from the iconic Eames Lounge Chair to the ergonomic Aeron office chair, Herman Miller has earned its reputation for making some of the best seats around. At upwards of $1,500, the Aeron is certainly an investment, but you can customize practically everything, from the arm pads to the casters. It’s available in three sizes, with several options for armrest adjustability, back support, and tilt.

WH Deputy Editor Eunice Lucero-Lee tested the medium-size Aeron in the Jasper colorway for two to four weeks, sitting for six to eight hours per workday. Lucero-Lee, who regularly experiences lower back pain, gave the chair a 5 out of 5.

Recent findings suggest that “This had perfect lumbar support for a whole eight-hour day's work,” she says. She also appreciated the adjustable armrests and how smoothly and quietly the wheels rolled while still offering enough traction and control. (The deep forest green colorway was another bonus.).

Instead of a traditional foam cushion, the Aeron features a breathable mesh seat that offers an almost weightless feeling. And the chair arrives fully assembled—as we'd expect at this price point.

While the steep price tag was Lucero-Lee’s biggest gripe, the Aeron’s customizable fit and excellent lumbar support make it a worthwhile splurge if you spend the better part of your day at your desk.

In a recent development, if you like to lean back and stretch your legs between meetings, the FlexiSpot ErgoX is worth checking out. Beyond customizable lumbar support, seat depth, and armrests, it features an adjustable headrest and a retractable footrest, so you can kick back and put your feet up while catching up on emails or taking a breather between calls.

Sources indicate that WH Fitness Reviews Editor Natascha Grief, who already owns a Herman Miller office chair, tested the ErgoX for over a month, sitting for six to eight hours per workday. While she initially found the back support a little uncomfortable, it took about a week for her to get used to sitting in a more upright position.

Industry observers note that “I think a good comparison would be switching to a pair of very supportive/corrective shoes after wearing pairs that are less structured,” she claims. Once she adjusted to the chair, she liked the firm back support and how the headrest helped her maintain a comfortable neck position.

It has been revealed that grief also loved how comfortable the chair was when fully reclined, though she found the mechanism for pulling out the footrest a little clunky. She ultimately gave the chair a 4 out of 5.

Considering how many adjustments and extras you're getting for the price, the ErgoX is a great option if you prefer a more supportive seat but still want the flexibility to kick back throughout the workday.

Like the Herman Miller Aeron, the Steelcase Gesture comes at a luxury price point, but its sturdy construction, supportive cushioning, and impressive range of adjustments help justify the investment. The chair comes in different materials and colors. Plus you can customize wheels for hard floors or carpet.

Of its many adjustable features, including recline and lumbar support, the most unique is its 360-degree armrests, which allow you to comfortably position your arms whether you're typing on your laptop or scrolling through your phone.

According to recent reports, after testing the Gesture for two to four weeks and sitting for two to four hours per workday, WH Managing Editor Laura McLaughlin gave it a 5 out of 5. She loved the firm seat cushion and how the chair managed to feel both stable and flexible.

“The back support specifically feels incredible, with firm yet comfortable padding and adjustable lumbar support,” she says.

It has been revealed that at nearly 60 pounds, the chair is on the heavier side, and McLaughlin found it surprisingly difficult to roll around. That said, she felt that its weight contributed to how sturdy and supportive it was.

The Gesture can also support up to 400 pounds, just like the Steelcase Series 2, and is backed by a 12-year warranty, which is reassuring when you're spending four figures on an office chair.

Recent findings suggest that if preserving your home’s interior design is top of mind, then the Branch Verve is minimalist with a unique flair and very comfortable. Made by the same brand as our top pick, this chair is $100 more and has fewer points of adjustment, but it also has a thick seat cushion and a breathable, beautifully designed 3D-knit back that comes in seven chic monochromatic looks.

Sources indicate that you can adjust lumbar support, seat depth, and tilt for a decent fit. The chair comes with an optional headrest for $59 more, and the armrests are height-adjustable as well as removable. The chair itself is on the heavier side, weighing in at 40 pounds, but it’s also Greenguard Gold certified, which means it has been tested for volatile organic compounds and chemical emissions.

Read More: Best Standing Desks For Walking Pads.

Industry observers note that for those who struggle with back pain, a supportive office chair can be the difference between a productive workday and injury. The Steelcase Series 2 is the best option for those folks because it’s weight-activated—you just sit, and the chair’s back tension adjusts to you.

The thick seat cushion relieves pressure, and you can adjust the height, width, and depth of the armrests. (Most office chair armrests are just adjustable by height and sometimes width.) The chair can also support up to 400 pounds, which is about 100 pounds more than most of our picks. In terms of design, you can choose between a variety of colors, two frame colors, an optional headrest, and wheels for carpet or hard flooring.

Read More: Uplift Kneeling Ergonomic Chair Review.

At under $500, the HON Ignition 2.0 is a budget office chair that still delivers in terms of support and adjustability. The chair itself is lightweight and easy to maneuver at under 25 pounds, and it sports a simple silhouette that won’t be an eyesore in your home office. The armrests can be raised and widened, and you can also easily adjust lumbar, tilt, and seat depth.

You can also opt to forgo armrests to bring the price closer to $400 or add a headrest and still keep the chair under the $600 threshold. The chair also comes backed by a limited lifetime warranty, which is unique for a high-quality home office chair. (For reference, the warranty on our top pick only lasts for seven years.).

At less than $100, the TikTok-famous Pukami Criss Cross Chair is a great option if you’re furnishing your home office on a budget. The extra-wide, foam-cushioned seat offers plenty of room to sit cross-legged, and its minimalist design and variety of color options make it easy to match with your home decor.

Industry observers note that despite its affordable price tag, the chair swivels, tilts, and can support up to 350 pounds. While it lacks the adjustable lumbar support, armrests, and wheels of our pricier picks, it’s worth considering if you work from home occasionally and don’t want to spend hundreds of dollars on an office chair.

Here are some key features to consider while you search for the best office chair for your body and needs.

In a recent development, office chairs are not one-size-fits-all, which is why adjustability is crucial. “Adjustability lets the chair match your body so your spine stays in a neutral, supported position,” indicates Dr. Gbolohan Okubadejo, a spine surgeon and the head of The Institute of Comprehensive Spine Care. The lumbar support should match the curve of your spine, and your feet should be able to sit flat on the floor, according to Okubadejo.

Sources indicate that “An unsupportive chair, or one that does not fit properly, can lead to chronic musculoskeletal injuries over time,” Lees says. “This may lead to pain that persists throughout the day, affecting sleep and stress levels. Long-term injuries may also include nerve damage that can lead to weakness or numbness.”.

Industry observers note that most home office chairs are height adjustable and have armrests that can be raised. If a chair has a headrest, which isn’t essential, that may be adjustable as well. “Being able to tweak depth, tilt, and lumbar support prevents hot spots and improves blood flow during long sits.” Okubadejo says. “Small adjustments through the day break up static strain, so muscles don’t fatigue and posture doesn’t collapse.”.

According to recent reports, lumbar refers to the lower back, and supporting this curve in your spine can relieve disc pressure and keep your pelvis in a neutral position, according to Okubadejo. “Good lumbar support lowers the risk of stiffness and pain during long hours at a desk,” he indicates.

Like chair height and seat cushioning, lumbar support will vary by person. “Postural muscles start to relax after a few minutes of sitting,” Lees says. “This leads to added stress on the spinal joints and extremity joints.” Luckily, many office chairs allow you to adjust the height and curve of the lumbar support. Okubadejo recommends options that can move up and down as well as in and out instead of stationary lumbar support.

The main components of a comfortable office chair are a sturdy frame, a thick seat cushion, and a supportive, breathable back. Most office chairs these days have a metal or plastic frame with a foam cushion and mesh back, although you can find upholstered and leather versions.

If you have the opportunity to test chairs in person, make sure that the seat is firm enough for you. “If the cushion is too soft, it won’t offer the support needed over time,” Lees claims. “A cushion that is too firm could create pressure points and possibly affect blood flow in the legs.”.

The materials of a chair can contribute to its overall weight and weight limit—both of which are notable to keep in mind during your search.

Office chairs, like our top pick from Branch, can be beautiful in their own right but not necessarily as stylish as a sofa or armchair. Unfortunately, you may need to prioritize comfort over design when working from home, but you can opt for chairs with upholstery-like materials or lots of color options to marry the two.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

IN THE TWO weeks since Robert Pattinson’s name was first mentioned in connection with James Bond—and in the handful of days since he was officially cast in the role—I’ve heard lots of talk about him as an actor, and him as a fit playing 007.

Sources indicate that these have been some of the easiest conversations I’ve had all year long, because, quite simply, Pattinson has been one of the best actors working for the last decade and counting. While his first big breaks came in the commendable space of films based on YA books (Harry Potter and Twilight), he’s long established himself at this point as an actor who can just about do it all, taking on a mix of projects big and small, characters good and evil. He’s shown a full capability run the full gauntlet from sane and noble to absolutely psychotic.

But I also recognize that not everyone is grinding out the indies from this year or the hidden gems from that year. Not everyone is even seeing the movies that some of us think of as the huge movies that everyone saw. But James Bond Casting is the kind of news everyone hears. And so I wanted to do my part to make sure everyone knows one thing only: Robert Pattinson rules.

Recent findings suggest that truly. There’s a common description for many cool actors: “He’s a character actor in a leading man’s body.” And no one seems more true to that than Pattinson, as his jawline cut from marble is often put to work in playing some of the most twisted and eccentric characters you’ll see in any movie. Hell, in 2026 alone, he’s already played a groom-to-be from hell in The Drama, a scheming villain in The Odyssey, and an ambitious 2000s television personality (a.k.a. To Catch a Predator’s Chris Hansen) in Primetime. And that’s not even to mention his role as the villain in Dune: Part Three (from his future Bond director Denis Villeneuve) coming later this year.

But that’s the glory of Pattinson, too—he clearly loves doing all that stuff, but he’s still the dashingly handsome, arrestingly charming guy on the surface, too. It’s a rare combination that makes him a unique star for our times; and clearly the significant studios agree, as he’s now been cast as two of contemporary movie culture’s most famous recurring roles, Batman and James Bond.

It has been revealed that he’s got a ton of great movies on his resume, ranging from blockbusters to little-seen independents, and almost all are worth your time. He’s even got small roles in some movies—like when he plays a professional driver for Julianne Moore in David Cronenberg’s Maps to the Stars—where he pops even as he tries to keep things grounded.

But I tried to keep it simple and get you ready for what makes him one of our very best, and a truly inspired Bond pick. So I stuck with six movies. That’s not too bad, right? A six-movie watchlist. Once you watch these six, you’ll get what you need to get about Robert Pattinson—and why he’s both one of the best actors working today, and a slam-dunk pick to play James Bond.

Sources indicate that pattinson went through a complicated process to become Bond that may or may not have involved being paid $1 million just to audition... but you can basically consider his role in Christopher Nolan’s Tenet as his first audition, and one all of us get to see. Nolan’s time-traveling espionage caper is a cool, sleek thriller that’s also a fast-paced battle to keep up with—and Pattinson’s Neil is the cool-as-a-cucumber agent who knows how to keep the whole thing grounded. He’s got great chemistry with the film’s lead, John David Washington, which may even give you ideas on how a Bond and Felix Leiter partnership could work out in a future film. Tenet is an extremely cool movie, and Pattinson is somehow the coolest thing about it.

Also see: Cosmopolis, probably Netflix’s The Take in early 2027.

In a recent development, while Pattinson has been doing impressive work for basically his whole career (even check out Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire!), it was Good Time—from directors Josh and Benny Safdie—that helped a lot of people in the moviegoing community wake up to just how good he’d become. This million-mile-a-minute crime story follows Connie (Pattinson) as he runs around in the seedy underbelly of New York City looking for money to bail him out of one terrible situation after another. In other words... it’s a Safdie movie. If you want to see how a Pattinson Bond could look as he deals with a mission gone awry or some other massive fuck-up, this is your movie.

Recent findings suggest that it’s not easy to put a whole movie on your back—and it’s even harder when it’s something that comes with massive expectations. In 2022’s The Batman, Pattinson became the latest actor to put his spin on Gotham City’s cave-dwelling vigilante, and, in typical Pattinson fashion, made him a character all his own. Where Pattinson shines is in the care he puts into both the Batman and Bruce Wayne personas; his early-career Batman is basically an ass-kicking noir detective, while his Bruce Wayne is kind of a brooding emo rich kid. The whole movie rocks, essentially a three-hour crime epic—but it’s easy to see why Amazon-MGM and director Denis Villeneuve felt comfortable putting their franchise on Pattinson’s bat armor-covered back.

It has been revealed that pattinson has also put in a lot of time playing creeps. In The Lighthouse, he plays a man stuck spending time with a grumpy, farting Willem Dafoe, and who eventually falls into his own descent, killing people and seagulls alike. And, well, he’s just not a great guy. Pattinson’s willingness to lose himself in a role, putting that psychosis front and center for all to see, marks an impressive willingness to both not be the hero, and to be vulnerable—which can also be great tools for someone as layered and complex as Bond tends to be.

Also see: The Odyssey, The Devil All the Time.

In a recent development, there’s another hallmark of Pattinson’s recent work: playing characters who, at one point or another, reveal themself to be freaky little freaks. Sometimes, like in James Gray’s The Lost City of Z, that’s evident from the jump, as he plays a bespectacled, bearded oddball. Other times, like in The Drama—which came out earlier this year and was a major hit for A24—he appears to be relatively normal at first, before eventually putting his antisocial behavior or extreme neuroses on display. The Drama is a wonderful character study, with Pattinson and Zendaya bouncing off each other marvelously, and it’s a thrill to watch Pattinson’s devolution into weirdo in a story that feels decidedly of the present. James Bond is a sleek, cool, spy, sure, but you don’t cast Robert Pattinson to just be a sleek, cool spy. Hopefully there’s a way for him to tap into his freak bona fides.

Also see: The Lost City of Z, Probably Dune: Part Three.

If you want to see Pattinson’s ability to be purely magnetic on screen, Primetime is the movie. Director Lance Oppenheim’s narrative debut is a thrilling and darkly comedic portrayal of ambition in the post-9/11 age of mid-aughts TV, and Pattinson leads the way as NBC’s Chris Hansen. He absolutely crushes every aspect of the role, making tens of choices with every single line and eating them all up like he’s at an all-you-can-eat buffet. He also bounces masterfully off costars Merritt Wever and Skyler Gisondo. The character is huge, narcissistic, and borderline evil, but Pattinson’s real skill is on display in making Hanson still never feel quite less than human. That’s a tricky balance beam to walk—but one he always manages to make look effortless.

Melissa Joan Hart Explains It All: Hot Flashes, Menopause, and Turning 50

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (950 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, actor Melissa Joan Hart has a vivid memory of her mother standing in front of their open freezer to cool off.
  • It has been revealed that “[She’s] only 20 years older than me, so maybe I missed the part where she was going through [menopause], but there was no conversation about it,” Hart told Healthline.
  • Her own perimenopausal symptoms started with night sweats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, actor Melissa Joan Hart has a vivid memory of her mother standing in front of their open freezer to cool off. As a child, she didn’t understand why. Now, as a 50-year-old woman, Hart knows that her mom was experiencing hot flashes.

It has been revealed that “[She’s] only 20 years older than me, so maybe I missed the part where she was going through [menopause], but there was no conversation about it,” Hart told Healthline. “I feel like it’s just becoming a hot topic with women, where…the taboo is going away from it now.”.

Her own perimenopausal symptoms started with night sweats.

“[It] was really jarring, and the first few times, you’re not really sure what that was…do I need to turn the air down or what’s going on here?” Hart said.

Over time, she learned that she was experiencing moderate to severe hot flashes, which affect up to 80% of women during the menopause transition and can persist for 7 to 10 years.

Doctors categorize hot flashes as mild, moderate, or severe, mentioned Diana Bitner, MD, OB-GYN, at Corewell Health.

“[So] if they’re mild, it’s a sense of warmth (maybe in the chest, or the neck, or the face). A moderate hot flash is where there’s associated sweating, and a severe hot flash is something that stops you in your tracks, wakes you up from the middle of the night,” Bitner told Healthline.

According to recent reports, hart has mostly experienced hot flashes while home or at her three sons’ activities, and they have yet to interfere with her work. However, according to research, one in three women report moderate to severe challenges in managing their work due to symptoms related to menopause.

Industry observers note that “It’s just so sad that about 10% of women leave the workforce due to menopause,” stated Bitner. “And so it can really affect our ability to perform at these key years of not only institutional memory, but also of earning power, and it can really affect the whole community.”.

Bitner remarked women should feel empowered to bring up their menopausal symptoms or questions with their doctor.

“[This] is something that was taboo for so long…women didn’t really talk about this, whether it was because of embarrassment, or [they] weren’t sure if anyone was experiencing it,” she remarked. “[There’s] no reason, in this day and age, we need to suffer through it…it’s something that there are treatment options for.”.

In fact, Bitner noted providing specific details about their symptoms, such as how many mild, moderate, or severe hot flashes they’ve experienced over the past week, can help doctors better assess patients’ needs.

Recent findings suggest that hart intends to discuss treatment options for her hot flashes with her doctor soon. In the last few years, she said she has put emphasis on her midlife health.

“I just was sick of waking up with aches and pains in general [thinking], ‘is this the rest of my life?’” she said.

She started listening to self-help books in the car while driving her kids around and found ways to put herself first.

Recent findings suggest that “My kids are a little bit older, so I kind of have that freedom to be able to do that,” she remarked. “[But] along with getting older, comes the menopause, comes that different time in life. And I think it’s a good time to reevaluate [how] our bodies can’t handle what [they] used to handle, and let’s figure it out.”.

Hart has partnered with pharmaceutical tech giant Bayer on its “Life Doesn’t Stop for a Hot Flash” campaign, which encourages women to discuss menopause symptoms with their doctors and promotes Lynkuet, a hormone-free prescription medication for moderate to severe hot flashes associated with menopause.

In a recent development, “It’s called ‘Life Doesn’t Stop for a Hot Flash’ campaign because it shouldn’t, because we should be able to push through, and this should be a time in our lives when our kids are getting older, and we’re able to kind of reinvent ourselves,” said Hart. “And I think it’s an exciting time, and it shouldn’t be something that we’re afraid of.”.

She is embracing speaking openly about midlife health.

“I hit 50 this year, and it was, like, a huge milestone, and I think that’s something to be proud of, and not something to shy away from,” she said.

Hart also hopes to challenge the longstanding barriers women face in Hollywood as they age, including fewer opportunities for leading roles.

“[I] think we’re seeing that the generation before, and my generation, it feels like we’re pushing those boundaries…and we’re saying, you know, that women at this age have a lot to give, have a lot of information to share, have a lot of stories to tell and experiences and adventures still ahead of us, and, you know, we’re not ready to stop,” Hart mentioned.

In everyday life, Bitner said that while some patients avoid talking about midlife issues like menopause with their doctors, she is seeing more patients who are confident being forthcoming.

As more women talk openly about menopause, she hopes to include men in the conversation, too. In fact, she invites her patients to bring their partners to appointments, so they can gain an understanding of menopause and the experiences their partners face, such as hot flashes, sleep problems, vaginal dryness, and discomfort or pain during intercourse.

“[Often], there’s, you know, comments that come up [from men who] say, ‘How do I talk about this without getting in trouble?’” noted Bitner. “[We] want everyone to join this conversation…it doesn’t have to be just her problem because we know it’s not.”.

Speaking of celebrities, Vintage Modern’s new Mustang-based Fastback is clearly based on a certain 2000s movie star. The hero car from the Nicolas Cage movie Gone in 60 Seconds, a Chip Foose–customized 1967 Mustang GT500, is well known in the enthusiast community as “Eleanor,” the car Cage couldn’t keep his hands off.

See all results for used cars for sale near 85395.

Sources indicate that to be clear, Vintage Modern isn’t saying its carbon-fiber-bodied creation is a take on the Eleanor Mustang, but there are plenty of similarities up to and including those massive front lower driving lights. However, underneath things aren’t 1967 but 2026 and newer, with the platform of a modern S650-chassis Mustang providing the basis for the build.

In a recent development, power starts from a standard 5.0-liter V-8 with 486 horsepower, paired with either a six-speed manual or a 10-speed automatic transmission. If you need more punch, perhaps for improbably enormous bridge jumps (professional driver, closed course), then a 3.0-liter Whipple supercharger ramps things up to a healthy 840 horsepower.

It has been revealed that overall, though, what you’re paying for with the Vintage Fastback is the build quality that comes with doing this kind of work for some time. Vintage Modern notes that each car represents 900 hours of assembly time, with hand-laid carbon-fiber panels and handcrafted assembly.

According to recent reports, no cost is mentioned at this point, though a quick look at what the Modern Classic truck costs indicates that those builds start at around the $250,000 mark. Since everything’s handmade apart from the mechanical bits, there’s an enormous amount of customization available, so you’re free to keep tacking on line items to that price.

Industry observers note that spending that kind of money on a Mustang is a certain kind of flex, but the Fastback’s blend of movie star looks and dependable modern underpinnings should be tempting for those with deep pockets and large Instagram followings. Just maybe lock the keys in a safe if you’re having Nic Cage over for lunch.

#75592. 4 Ways to Support Eating Disorder Recovery This Holiday Season

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1232 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

4 Ways to Support Eating Disorder Recovery This Holiday Season

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1232 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.
  • The holidays are about spending time with friends and family, traditions, and meals.
  • In a recent development, even someone who's made considerable progress in their eating disorder recovery can find themselves plagued by eating disorder thoughts or anxious about situations which previously would have been quite manageable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

The holidays are about spending time with friends and family, traditions, and meals. For someone in recovery from an eating disorder, though, the changes in routine, new foods, and comments about eating and weight can make what is supposed to be an enjoyable time feel overwhelming.

In a recent development, even someone who's made considerable progress in their eating disorder recovery can find themselves plagued by eating disorder thoughts or anxious about situations which previously would have been quite manageable. Family can be a source of this stress, especially when the subject of dieting, exercise, and appearance comes up.

In my work as a psychotherapist specializing in eating disorders, I've found that most family members and friends genuinely want to be supportive. But even with the best intentions, they may not realize how their words or actions affect someone in recovery. Here are four ways loved ones can offer support during the holidays.

How many times do you have conversations about food and weight over the holidays? Someone will be saying they're going to skip breakfast so they've got room for dinner. Someone else will be talking about their Fresh Year’s resolution to lose weight. A relative will comment on someone's looks or joke about having to go to the gym after dessert.

In a recent development, these comments are so ubiquitous that we tend to just ignore them. For someone in the eating disorder recovery process, though, those same comments can be a reinforcement of the very beliefs they're trying to dismantle (that certain foods are "bad," that you have to "earn" your food, that your body size is a measure of your worth, etc.). Try to avoid commenting on what other people are eating, how much they're eating, or whether their bodies have changed. This includes compliments about weight loss. You may not know why someone's weight has changed, and what you think is "just being nice" may actually reinforce eating disorder thoughts and behaviors. These comments also contribute to weight bias and stigma.

Pay attention to how you talk about your own eating, too. Describing yourself as "bad" for having dessert, or saying you're going to have to make it up, sends the message that eating is something you should feel guilty about.

If another family member is starting to go down the diet-calories-and-body line of thinking, consider changing the subject. The person in eating disorder recovery doesn't necessarily have to be the one to speak up and set that boundary.

It has been revealed that holiday meals don't always happen at predictable times. Dinner may be served several hours later than usual, people may skip meals in anticipation of a large gathering, or there may be an expectation that everyone should eat at the same time.

In a recent development, for someone in the recovery phase from an eating disorder, eating regularly throughout the day may be an essential part of the treatment. They may need a snack just before the main holiday meal, or may need to eat when the rest of the family are skipping a meal because they want to leave room for dinner.

In a recent development, comments like "You'll spoil your appetite" or "Can't you just wait until dinner?" can make an already stressful situation more difficult. What may be a very minor change in intends to someone without an eating disorder may be much more complicated for someone working to establish regular eating patterns.

Industry observers note that if you're hosting, consider asking ahead of time whether there's anything you can do to help. You don't need to make an announcement or draw attention to someone's eating. Simply having food available in case they need to eat when others aren't can be helpful.

Unless you're directly involved in supporting your loved one's meal initiative as part of their treatment, avoid monitoring their portions or questioning what they're eating. Even when it comes from a place of concern, having someone watch what you eat can increase anxiety and self-consciousness, making eating even more difficult.

Sources indicate that when someone you love has an eating disorder, it's understandable that you might worry about how they're doing. You may wonder whether they're eating enough, how treatment is going, or whether they're struggling more than they're letting on.

It has been revealed that when you're together for the holidays, though, try not to let concerns about your loved one's eating disorder dominate your interactions. Eating disorders can take up so much time and mental energy that people may lose interest in activities they once enjoyed, withdraw from relationships, or have difficulty engaging in everyday life. But that doesn't mean every conversation needs to revolve around their eating disorder or how they're doing in treatment.

Talk about things other than food and recovery. Ask about a show they're watching, a book they've read, a movie they've enjoyed, or something else that might interest them. Include them in family conversations and traditions, even if they seem less engaged than they used to be. The idea is to give them opportunities to connect with others without feeling pressured to participate or having every conversation come back to their eating disorder.

According to recent reports, there's a lot of pressure to enjoy the holidays. We're supposed to look forward to family gatherings, appreciate time together, and participate in traditions that are meant to be fun. But the holidays can also bring up anxiety, grief, loneliness, and difficult family dynamics.

Sources indicate that for someone in eating disorder recovery, these feelings may be accompanied by anxiety around food and body image or guilt after eating. They may want to be part of the celebration while also feeling desperate to avoid certain aspects of it.

In a recent development, if they say they're having a hard time, you may want to offer reassurance and try to convince them there's nothing to worry about. "It's only one meal," "Just relax," "Don't let that ruin your holiday," etc., are all things people say with the best of intentions but can quite often leave the person feeling misunderstood or frustrated with themselves for having the difficulty they do.

According to recent reports, instead of trying to convince them they shouldn't feel anxious, acknowledge what they're experiencing. You might say, "I know these gatherings can be stressful" or "I'm glad you're here, even though I know this isn't easy." You can also ask whether they'd like some company, want to talk, or need a little space.

Feeling anxious or uncomfortable doesn't necessarily mean someone isn't making progress in their eating disorder recovery. They may be working hard to participate in a holiday meal or eat foods they've previously avoided, even when eating disorder thoughts are especially loud. These experiences can take a lot of effort, and being able to face that discomfort without turning to familiar eating disorder behaviors is an key part of recovery.

The holidays can be especially challenging for someone with an eating disorder. Being mindful of your words and behaviors, supporting their treatment, and continuing to include them in family traditions can help them feel supported and connected to the people and experiences they care about.

The 10 Best Fitness Trackers for Women, Tested and Reviewed by Editors

📅 06 Nov 2018 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3927 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in.
  • Finding the right fitness tracker is less about buying the most advanced wearable out there and more about choosing the one that will actually work for how you’ll use it to help you meet your fitness goals.
  • For this guide, we considered a range of fitness trackers for different training styles and tracking needs, from simple bands for everyday activity tracking to running watches, smartwatches, screenless wearables, and smart rings, all designed to monitor sleep, recovery, fitness, and health trends over time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Finding the right fitness tracker is less about buying the most advanced wearable out there and more about choosing the one that will actually work for how you’ll use it to help you meet your fitness goals. You may want a smartwatch that can handle calls and texts along with fitness data tracking, or maybe you’re looking for a distraction-free screenless band that quietly tracks your metrics in the background. If running is your thing, you may want a smartwatch with GPS accuracy and real-time training metrics that are easy to read during a run, and if you’re focused on improving sleep, you may prefer a smart ring that won’t feel bulky overnight.

For this guide, we considered a range of fitness trackers for different training styles and tracking needs, from simple bands for everyday activity tracking to running watches, smartwatches, screenless wearables, and smart rings, all designed to monitor sleep, recovery, fitness, and health trends over time.

Whoop earned the top spot for the best overall fitness tracker because it provides deeper understanding of your data while also giving context of what all that data means. I’ve been using a Whoop for the past several years, and of all the fitness tracker options I’ve tested, it remains my hands-down favorite. It delivers some of the most useful recovery, sleep, and strain insights in a distraction-free design that’s so comfortable I often completely forget that I’m wearing it. The battery life is impressive, and I only have to charge mine twice a month.

Sources indicate that whoop 5.0 is built on the foundation of an app that offers analysis of your metrics paired with context, so you actually learn what all the numbers mean for your health and training. The screen-free design means that instead of buzzing constantly or encouraging you to check another display, it quietly tracks your metrics in the background and turns that data into recovery, strain, sleep data to give you an overall picture of your fitness within an app.

The sensor platform uses multi-wavelength optical heart rate sensors, skin-temperature sensing, blood oxygen monitoring, and accelerometer and gyroscope motion sensors to collect data continuously, tracking your resting heart rate, heart rate variability, respiratory rate, blood oxygen, skin temperature, sleep stages, strain, and recovery.

The app then interprets those numbers, in a way that feels more actionable than raw data alone, to generate a daily readiness score that indicates how much physical exertion your body is up for on any given day (00033though it’s always key to listen to your body regardless of what a wearable notes). If you wake up with a low recovery score, for example, Whoop may recommend reducing workout intensity. If your sleep debt is climbing, it will show how much rest you need to get back on track.

It also offers other behavior change suggestions that could improve how you feel based on the data it collects about you and your habits over time. In fact, the in-depth habit tracking feature offers some of the most valuable insights into how day-to-day behaviors affect us physiologically. As a trainer, this has been one of the features I've seen make the most long-term impact with clients, as it really helps them connect the dots and understand how everything is interrelated.

Whoop 5.0 does require a membership and there are three different tiers, the main difference being the level of insights and analysis. Whoop One covers the core Whoop experience, including sleep, strain, recovery, steps, activity monitoring, heart-rate tracking, and women’s hormonal insights, which helps us see how menstrual cycle phases may relate to sleep, recovery, and performance. Whoop Peak adds a broader health and wellness layer, including health monitor, stress monitor, healthspan, and more advanced coaching-style insights for users who want to connect daily habits with longer-term performance and recovery trends (this is the tier I personally go with). Whoop Life is the most advanced tier, adding heart-health features such as ECG, irregular heart rhythm notifications, and blood pressure insights where available. Ultimately, the difference between the tiers is less about the tracker experience itself and more about how much interpretation, health context, and advanced monitoring you want.

Sources indicate that the tradeoff is cost. Since Whoop uses a membership model, it will end up being more expensive over time than a tracker that doesn’t require a subscription. It also is not the best choice if you want live pace, distance, or workout stats on your wrist during a run. For that, a Garmin, Apple Watch, Samsung Galaxy Watch, or COROS watch will be more practical.

Sources indicate that the Google Fitbit Inspire earned its spot as the best budget pick because it gives you the core fitness-tracking features most people want in a slim and approachable design. It’s not trying to be a full smartwatch or a performance running watch. Instead, it focuses on the basics: steps, heart rate, workouts, sleep, active minutes, and general wellness trends.

Industry observers note that that simplicity makes the Fitbit Inspire a good entry point for someone who wants to become more aware of their fitness data without getting buried in advanced metrics. It can track walks, gym workouts, casual runs, and sleep, while the Fitbit app makes the data easy to understand. You can rapidly see how much movement you got throughout the day, how long you slept, and how your habits are trending over time. Additionally, you’ll get a stress management score, guided breathing sessions, and reminders to move.

According to recent reports, it is also one of the easiest trackers to wear all day. The band is slim enough to feel less bulky than a smartwatch, and the display is small but still easy to use for checking basic stats. If your main goals are walking more, staying accountable, improving sleep habits, or getting started with activity tracking, the Inspire offers strong value.

Industry observers note that the main limitation is that it’s not necessarily built for serious training. Depending on the model, the GPS may rely on your phone rather than being fully built into the device, and runners who want advanced pace analysis, training load, recovery guidance, or race tools will likely outgrow it. But for the price, it’s one of the most practical fitness trackers for everyday use.

Industry observers note that the Apple Watch Series 12 blends health tracking, workout features, smartwatch convenience, and safety tools better than almost any other wearable. If you already use an iPhone, this is the most seamless option in our guide.

Recent findings suggest that the Series 12 features more advanced sensor capabilities, including an upgraded optical heart sensor that measures heart rate every five seconds, and tracks HRV more frequently. WH associate fitness editor Addison Aloin wrote in her review that the Series 12 has “a great baseline of health and fitness features.”.

Recent findings suggest that the Series 12 tracks a wide range of workouts, including running, walking, cycling, strength training, HIIT, yoga, Pilates, swimming, hiking, and many more. During activity, the display is bright and you can easily view data like pace, distance, heart rate, time, and workout zones during runs and workouts. It also integrates smoothly with Apple Fitness+, the Health app, and third-party training apps.

One of the most meaningful updates the Series 12 got is a new readiness score, which uses recent activity, training load, your sleep score, and overnight metrics like heart rate, respiratory rate, skin temperature, and recovery HRV to estimate how prepared your body is for exertion. The score runs from 0 to 10 and gives you a recommendation for your day, such as Recover, Pace Yourself, Ready, or Go For It. “My only complaint is that it’s kind of hard to find the readiness score on the watch and in the Health app,” Aloin indicates.

Since it’s so much more than just a tracker you wear during workout, the Apple Watch also offers a lot of versatility. It can handle notifications, calls, music, maps, timers, contactless payments, fall detection, and emergency features, making it a strong option for anyone who wants one device that can move between workouts and everyday life.

It is also a good pick for people who like motivational nudges. Apple’s activity rings are simple, visual, and surprisingly effective if you respond well to daily goals. If you want coaching-style feedback without digging through complex training dashboards, the Series 12’s newer software can translate health and fitness data into easily digestible prompts.

Recent findings suggest that the Series 12 offers up to 24 hours of everyday battery life, and Apple says 15 minutes of charging can add up to 12 hours of battery. That makes it more manageable for overnight sleep tracking, but it still requires more planning than fitness trackers that last several days or longer on a single charge. “I’ve found the battery life is awesome for everyday use, but usually does need a charge every other day or so,” Aloin says.

Read More: Apple Watch Series 12 vs. Ultra 4.

The Google Fitbit Air gives you the quiet, distraction-free experience of a screenless wearable at a more approachable price point than premium recovery bands. The Fitbit Air tracks core metrics like activity, heart rate, sleep, and wellness trends over time, then sends that information to your phone.

Since there’s no screen, you’re not checking your wrist throughout the day. That makes it a strong option for anyone who wants to be more mindful about movement and sleep but doesn’t want a smartwatch. It’s also a good fit for people who are curious about screenless tracking but are not ready to commit to a more expensive platform. It offers a simpler, lower-pressure way to see whether passive health tracking actually helps your routine.

In a recent development, the Fitbit app is another advantage. Fitbit’s platform is approachable, especially for beginners, and tends to present health data in a way that feels less intimidating than more athlete-focused apps. That makes the Air a strong choice for casual customers who want guidance without performance overload.

According to recent reports, the main limitation is that a screenless budget tracker will not replace a running watch or smartwatch. You will not get the same real-time workout stats, app support, phone features, or advanced training analysis. But if you want affordable, low-distraction tracking, Fitbit Air is a compelling pick.

Sources indicate that the Coros Pace 4 is our best lightweight pick because it delivers serious training features in a watch that feels easy to wear. After testing the watch for two months, MH deputy features editor Carina Hsieh said that it feels so lightweight that you forget it’s there. It’s especially appealing for runners and fitness-minded users who want more data than a basic tracker can provide but don’t want a bulky smartwatch.

In a recent development, coros has built a strong reputation among runners because its watches tend to offer excellent battery life, practical training tools, and reliable GPS. The Pace 4 continues that tradition. “I was pleasantly surprised by how responsive and quick the GPS signal was on runs,” Hsieh remarked. She also noted that the watch had an exceptionally long battery life during her testing, and that she only had to charge it twice in two months.

In a recent development, for runners, the Pace 4 can track pace, distance, heart rate, route data, workouts, recovery, and training trends. Features like race predictions, virtual pacing, breadcrumb navigation, and personalized training tools make it feel like a strong contender for anyone who is a serious runner. It is also useful for people who cross-train, since it can handle gym workouts, cycling, walking, and other activities.

A big reason to choose the Pace 4 over other smartwatches is that it feels purpose-built for fitness. You’re not paying for a huge app ecosystem or phone-like features. Instead, you’re getting a lightweight training watch that can help you understand your fitness, recovery, and progress.

The Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 is the best fitness tracker for Android users, especially anyone with a Samsung Galaxy phone. It offers a polished smartwatch experience with robust health and fitness tools, making it a bit like an Android equivalent to the Apple Watch. WH beauty editor Nicole Saunders, who has tested multiple wearables over the years, says she usually struggles to wear trackers consistently because the bands were uncomfortable overnight. But the Galaxy Watch 9 changed that. “The band is surprisingly comfortable to wear and, dare I say, actually looks good,” she stated.

This smartwatch tracks everyday activity, steps, heart rate, workouts, stress, sleep, and recovery-style metrics. It also includes Samsung’s Vitals feature, which monitors overnight patterns including heart rate, respiratory rate, blood oxygen, skin temperature, and other sleep-related signals, then compares them against your personal baseline. Saunders says it took about a full week for her baseline to set up, and anything outside of her normal range appeared in orange in the app, making it easy to compare metrics and spot subtle changes over time.

It also tracks a wide range of exercise modes, and its running features are useful for people who want coaching-style tools. Samsung’s body composition measurement feature can also be helpful for observing trends over time, though the numbers should be treated as estimates rather than medical-grade measurements. Saunders also liked the sleep features, including sleep quality tracking and snore detection, which she found both funny and potentially useful for better understanding nighttime habits.

Recent findings suggest that the watch pairs easily with Galaxy phones, and the Samsung Health app organizes fitness and wellness data in an approachable way. If you want a tracker that can monitor workouts in the morning, handle notifications during the day, and track sleep at night, the Galaxy Watch 9 is a strong choice. In her testing, Saunders found it to be stylish and effective, adding that it would make a great gift for someone starting a health journey or looking for more detailed insights.

It has been revealed that the Oura Ring 5 offers robust health and sleep tracking in the most discreet package of all the fitness trackers in this guide. If you don’t like wearing a watch around the clock or simply prefer jewelry over a wristband, Oura is the easiest fitness tracker to live with. In her review, WH associate editor Olivia Luppino mentioned it’s the only fitness tracker she’s ever used that she hasn’t wanted to take off.

In a recent development, the Oura Ring’s biggest strength is passive health tracking. It’s designed to unobtrusively monitor your body in the background, and then translate that information into readiness, sleep, activity, stress, temperature, and recovery insights in an easy to use app. It can be especially helpful for people who want to understand how sleep, illness, stress, menstrual cycle changes, and daily habits affect energy.

For sleep tracking, the Ring 5 is one of the more comfortable options since a ring is less bulky than a watch, and many people find it easier to wear overnight. The app also makes sleep data easy to understand, showing not just how long you slept but how restorative that sleep may have been.

The tradeoff is workout tracking. Oura can track activity and has improved its fitness features, but it’s still not the best choice for people who want real-time stats during runs, strength workouts, or cycling sessions. It can also interfere with grip during weightlifting and kettlebell training. If you want to glance at pace, heart rate, or intervals mid-workout, choose a watch. If you want discreet, all-day and all-night health tracking, choose a smart ring.

For runners, the Garmin Forerunner 570 sits in a sweet spot between advanced training watches and an everyday wearable. Garmin makes several excellent Forerunner models, but the 570 offers a mix of running metrics, GPS tools, recovery insights, smartwatch features, and comfortable wearability for runners who want more than the basics without jumping straight to flagship option.

Sources indicate that the Forerunner 570 is designed to be useful for structured training with its capability to track runs, intervals, long runs, tempo sessions, races, recovery runs, and cross-training workouts. It also gives runners access to Garmin’s broader training ecosystem, including performance metrics, suggested workouts, recovery guidance, HRV status, sleep data, training readiness-style insights, and race-related tools. For someone training for a 5K, half marathon, marathon, or simply trying to become a more consistent runner, those features can be super useful.

It has a bright AMOLED display, touchscreen support as well as physical buttons, a feature that’s especially notable for runners since touchscreens can sometimes be frustrating with sweat, rain, or gloves. Battery life varies from 8 hours to up to 10 days depending on how many features you’re using.

The biggest drawback is price. Though it’s not the priciest Forerunner offering out there, the Forerunner 570 is not inexpensive, and newer runners who only want pace, distance, and heart rate may be perfectly happy with a more affordable Forerunner model. But runners who want a capable watch they won’t outgrow, the 570 is a great option.

In a recent development, the Garmin Cirqa is the best screenless tracker for lovers of the Garmin fitness ecosystem, since it integrates seamlessly with Garmin’s other tech. It delivers health and activity tracking without adding another display to your life, and is especially well suited for anyone who wants to use Garmin Connect but doesn't want to wear a full Garmin watch all day long.

Sources indicate that that makes Cirqa especially useful for athletes who already own a Garmin running, cycling, or outdoor watch. You may want to wear your Forerunner for workouts and during runs, but prefer something smaller and screen-free for sleep, recovery, or everyday tracking. The Cirqa fills that gap.

Recent findings suggest that it also has a cost advantage over some screenless competitors because it doesn’t require a subscription. That makes it appealing for Garmin loyalists who want ongoing tracking without committing to a monthly membership.

In a recent development, the Cirqa isn’t the best choice if you want live workout stats, on-wrist coaching, or a display for pace and distance, and a Garmin watch would be better for that. But as a low-distraction daily tracker that complements Garmin’s training platform, Cirqa is a welcome addition to the category.

The Google Fitbit Edge bridges the gap between a simple Fitbit band and a full smartwatch, making it a strong choice if you want a display but don’t want a bulkier smartwatch. It gives you a screen for checking stats, starting workouts, reviewing progress, and seeing basic information at a glance.

Recent findings suggest that compared with the Fitbit Air, the Edge is more interactive, compared with the Inspire, it’s a more advanced option, and compared with a Pixel Watch, it’s simpler to use and more fitness focused. It offers enough features to be useful throughout the day, tracking activity, workouts, sleep, heart-rate trends, and daily wellness data, while still keeping the overall experience lighter than a smartwatch. If you want a compact Google Fitbit tracker with a screen and stronger features than the entry-level models, the Edge is the best fit.

Industry observers note that A good heart rate monitor is one of the most important features to look for in a fitness tracker, whether you’re training seriously or just getting started. Heart rate data can help you better understand exercise intensity, track effort during workouts, and monitor resting heart rate over time, which can be a useful marker of cardiovascular fitness. While wrist-based trackers typically aren’t as precise as chest straps, they can still offer a helpful read on exertion levels during moderate to intense activity, according to a 2019 study in Cardiovascular Diagnosis & Therapy.

Industry observers note that sleep tracking can be a useful feature because sleep plays a major role in recovery, energy, mood, and overall performance. By tracking patterns like sleep duration, consistency, and overnight restlessness, a fitness tracker can help you spot habits that may be affecting how you feel the next day. Many models also break down sleep stages, show trends over time, and offer recovery or readiness insights based on your nightly data. While the numbers aren’t always perfect, they can provide a helpful starting point for understanding your routine and making small changes, like adjusting bedtime, limiting late caffeine, or improving sleep consistency.

Weight may not seem that notable at first, but it matters when you’re wearing a fitness tracker all day and night. A larger, heavier model can feel more noticeable over time, especially during sleep or long workouts. There’s no single ideal size, and the best option will depend on how you initiative to use it.

Recent findings suggest that if you run, hike, or spend a lot of time outdoors, it may be worth choosing a more durable model, even if it’s slightly bulkier. For everyday wear, walking, strength training, or mostly indoor workouts, a lighter, lower-profile tracker may be more comfortable. Ultimately, the right fit comes down to your activity level, wrist size, and what you’ll actually want to keep wearing.

It has been revealed that many of the best fitness trackers can run for days or even weeks on a single charge, such as the Whoop 5.0. But battery doesn't always equate to quality, given that an option like the Apple Watch Series 12 needs to be charged every day and it’s still one of our absolute favorites. Ultimately it comes down to how a trackers charging needs will fit into your routine.

In a recent development, as with all tech, you want a fitness tracker that’s easy to use. If your upcoming tracker isn’t intuitive for you to set up or use daily, you’re far less likely to use it consistently. Ultimately, the only way to know for sure is to try it out yourself to see if it works for you. That's why it’s smart to buy a fitness tracker with a generous return policy.

I’ve been a certified personal trainer for more than a decade, and together with other Women’s Health editors, I’m constantly testing the latest fitness trackers across key factors like durability, comfort, features, and accuracy. We tested them during our workouts, on our runs, in Pilates class, and more. And of course, we tested them during sleep. Whether you’re training regularly or just want something for everyday activity tracking, the models we tested for the latest update range from basic fitness trackers to powerful smartwatches and everything in between.

Industry observers note that I USED TO think chinos were the kind of pants your dad wore to a backyard barbecue in the early 2000s. You know—the stiff, boxy khaki pants sitting way too high on the waist that ended up looking like high-waters. But chinos have come a long way since then. These days, chinos look cleaner, fit better, and feel more comfortable than most denim I own. I can wear them to the office with a button-down, out to dinner with a blazer, or just throw them on with a tee and sneakers for a Yankees game.

Recent findings suggest that most of today’s styles now come with stretchy fabrics and moisture-wicking tech, and lightweight materials that make them way easier to wear year-round. Since 2020, the Men’s Health fashion team and I have tested more than 50 pairs—from slim-fit classics to more relaxed cuts—to find the chinos that belong in rotation. Without further ado, browse our selection with picks from Bonobos, Everlane, and Lululemon to find one that suits your style and elevates your everyday wardrobe.

After thoroughly putting Lululemon's ABC Pant to the test, I found that it flat-out outshines everything else in its class. The sweat-wicking, quick-drying, and wrinkle-resistant fabric with four-way stretch makes this pair feel like your favorite joggers disguised as office pants. Unlike the others on the list, it comes with their proprietary ABC (Anti-Ball Crushing) design. Our editors found it's basically a clever gusset that eases tension in the crotch and thigh area, so you never feel squeezed or restricted when you're walking or sitting for hours.

After owning this pair since 2020, its performance has never let us down once. The elastomultiester-polyester fabric blend makes it feel technical yet polished. It moves like activewear but looks structured enough for meeting or semi-dressy events. During brutal summer commutes, we stayed dry and comfortable, never dealing with that dreaded swampy feeling below deck.

The classic fit hits right in the middle, meaning not too slim, not too loose, and comes in a bunch of office-approved colors that look sharp from 9 to 5 and beyond. We've worn this pair everywhere: happy hours, long-haul flights, work dinners, the list goes on. Functionally, Lululemon thought of everything: hand pockets that don't bulge, a hidden zip pocket for your wallet, and even a side pocket to keep your phone secure while you're on the move.

Lululemon’s ABC pant is what guys wish their everyday slacks felt like—unrestrictive, clean as a whistle, and ridiculously comfortable.

Industry observers note that visible creases in your pants can be a pain, cramping your style and throwing off that polished look you’re going for. It has been revealed that what's the next best thing close to slim-fit chino? Ding-ding-ding, skinny-fit. That is, one that's not constricting on your lower half. Before you jump ship, this pair from J.Crew isn't super tight like the skinny jeans that peaked in the early 2000s. For starters, it's infused with the brand's stretch technology that provides a subtle yet noticeable amount of give—to move every which way without feeling stiff and eliminate any annoying break-in period. According to recent reports, also, the structured twill-lined waistband with chambray binding adds a touch of durability and style, while the angled pockets offer easy access to your most valuable items. Let's not forget how versatile they are, too. This style works at the bar, the office, and even on the golf course. Rhone totally gets it right with workout clothes, but the athleisure brand also has the everyday chinos down pat as well. We love that the fabric actually uses lyocell to amplify breathability and smoothness, which is comparable to the texture of silk. Designed for office professionals, the pants also boast a media pouch for your phone and a security zipper pocket for your cardholder.
